#8259. Mountain Lions, Wildfires, & Volcanoes: Washington Finally

After our longest day on the PCT (46 miles!) we took a well-deserved rest at a spa hotel with Nina and Rebecca. We sleep in, soak in the hot tub until we’re pruney, and eat as much as we can. There’s no laundry onsite so we wash our clothes in the bathtub and hang them to dry outside. After our attempt at running I have shin splints. My back chafed under the unfamiliar day pack and my skin is tender. Other than those issues and the expected fatigue, we’re mostly unscathed from our monumentous effort.

We spend time in the hotel prepping for our last few weeks on trail. We mail home items we’d shipped up to Portland from further down the trail, and I switch my film camera out for my mirrorless one. Finally, we’re ready to get to it.

We head to Cascade Locks and see some hiker pals out in town. They’re planning to stick around for PCT Trail Days. We had debated staying, but it would be another several days before the event starts and we don’t want to stick around that long.

We bid farewell to Nina and Rebecca and walk across the Bridge of the Gods, officially entering our last state of the PCT. The gorge is beautiful and windy and crossing the Columbia River via foot is a new experience.

We quickly enter the woods on the Washington side and begin to climb. The path is lined with blackberries and poison oak. One is good for snacking as we walk, the other we avoid. We’ve started to see many Southbound hikers at this point making their way into Cascade Locks for Trail Days. The trail quickly becomes hot and humid and we’re sweaty as we make our way uphill, climbing out of the gorge.

Now that we’re finally in Washington, it feels like the soap bubble has popped. The fires we’ve been hearing about are no longer far away. We have about 500 miles left of the PCT, something we’d accomplish in a few short weeks at our current pace if we could. But, we have to face the music – we can’t. The trail to the North of Snoqualmie Pass is closed up to Stevens Pass, and then the trail North of Rainy Pass to the Northern Terminus is closed as well. That’s about 100 miles of the remaining trail we cannot do. There are alternates, which we discuss ad nauseam. Should we go around the Snoqualmie closure and keep a continuous footpath? Should we end the hike at Rainy, and go to the border later? Should we break our footpath and just hike the available PCT miles? Or should we attempt an alternate? The SOBOs (southbound hikers) are bringing us news of poor air quality around Stevens Pass and Snoqualmie Pass and our lungs took a beating already in Oregon. I don’t want to hike alternates through Washington in poor air quality just to reach a border – that feels like it would be a pointless exercise in suffering. And on top of it all, we live in Washington. We are getting closer to home every day, and some of the alternates bring me less than an hour away from my house by car. I can’t imagine road walking in the smoke and being so close to home. It would be unenjoyable and not at all how I’d want to end my hike. At this point we’ve been hiking for almost 130 days. We have run out of things to talk about, so discussing what to do and how we’d feel about each option occupies most of our days.

We push on through Southern Washington. The forested trails can be humid and have more climbing that we’d seen in Oregon. We’re both feeling the effects of our huge day well into the next week. We are exhausted and end each day with less miles than planned. The scenery is nice though, and we get glimpses of the volcanos. One day we take an alternate to see a waterfall, and camp next to a group of popular lakes. With our shorter miles we arrive at camp earlier. Its nice to enjoy eating in the daylight and hanging around at camp. We even have time to swim.

My coworker Thom offered to bring us a re-supply outside of Trout Lake. This will keep us from having to take a day off trail, which will help keep our momentum going. He has also offered to bring us “freshies” and we send him a list of our current cravings. We hike to meet him at a trailhead and find a feast set up for us. He makes us meatball subs and has fresh fruit for us to devour. We sit in comfortable chairs for hours. While we skipped the popular town of Trout Lake, we’re happy with the quick detour. We’ve seen the town before and if we’d gotten off trail we fear we might not have gotten back on. This was also part of our reasoning for skipping Trail Days. Many of our friends who went decided to end their hike at Cascade Locks. The fires were too much to navigate, and people want to enjoy Washington. I don’t blame them.

We depart our personal re-supply stop with an extra special late birthday gift – fully cooked, shelf stable bacon. We mix it in with our pasta and have some for breakfast the next day. It hits the spot.

Thom’s resupply helped us with getting enough food to make it to White Pass. We head North, excited to pass by Mount Adams and through the Goat Rocks Wilderness. As we hike on, the first of the hikers getting back on trail from Trail Days start to filter in and we get to camp with thru hikers again. We get a bit of cell service and I immediately check Watch Duty – one of my most used apps right now. I see that there’s another fire, this one on the PCT. The trail between Steven’s Pass and Steheiken is closed now. Our hearts sink and its a sad evening. We now have only two options – take alternate routes for the entire last 250 miles of trail, or get off the trail at Snoqualmie Pass.

We head into the Mount Adams Wilderness with heavy hearts. The burn scars feel a bit more tragic than normal. We’ve been hiking apart more and more lately, just walking in our thoughts. I’m trailing Sarah by a few minutes, listening to my audiobook when I hear her say “STOP.” I stop dead in my tracks and look around. She’s ahead at the top of a small hill. I join her and she says she just saw a large mountain lion heading into the copse of trees to the left of where the trail wraps around a bend. We walk together, making noise and scanning the surroundings. We pass the trees and see a small cat hopping around playfully in the underbrush. “I thought you saw a big cat….” I say. “I did.” she responds.

The implication that the mother to this young mountain lion is somewhere nearby sinks in. We stand back to back and make our way down the trail. We don’t see another cat, but we hike within sight of each other for the rest of the trail.

The Mount Adams wilderness is gorgeous. We cross glacial streams, take in the massive mountain views, and see the sunset on the glaciers. It passes by so quickly, and before 2 days are over we’ve put the mountain behind us.

We enter the Goat Rocks Wilderness, a highly anticipated section for us. We’ve made plans to come here both when we’ve lived in Oregon and Washington and they’ve never panned out. The smoke forecast looks good and we’re excited for epic views. We push through another grueling, humid climb, exiting the forest to an amazing meadow. The trail continues to climb up to Cispus Pass. We marvel at the scenery. It feels like we’re in a different world. After crossing the pass we descend into another meadow. There are endless wildflowers and an icy stream flowing through our path. We look high up onto the rocks and see goats!! It feels like a fairytale. We set an early alarm for the next morning and watch the sunset reflect off of Mount Adams.

The next day we start hiking early and are glad of it. There’s an incredible inversion and the smoke layer has settled enough to give us good views.

We climb up towards Old Snowy mountain, pausing every few steps to turn around and take in Mount Adams. We can see Mount Saint Helen’s as well, and tons of wildflowers. We reach continue to climb and reach a turnoff to Old Snowy. We aren’t going to summit the peak, but we are going to take the alternate that brings us up closer to the summit and skips a sketchy, icy snow traverse. There’s a small bit of snow to navigate on the alternate but it isn’t nearly as steep as the one we’re skipping. Then we’re on shale, getting epic views of Mount Rainier. Sadly, we can see the smoke in the surrounding peaks from here as well. I know if the air was clear, we’d be able to see much more.

We descend, and the loose gravelly stone is a challenge. The steep exposure doesn’t help our footing. We’re much slower than normal but the views are epic. We make our way back onto the main PCT and hit the Knife’s Edge, a famous section of trail. It’s incredible but the loose footing is still sketchy.

Finally we get back onto dirt and cross more picturesque meadows. We add this as another place to return to soon, this one actually reasonably close to home. As we descend we consult our maps on the remaining distance to the White Pass Cracker Barrel. According to FarOut, the gas station closes at 6 and showers and laundry close at 5. We’re going to have to hoof it if we want either of those things in addition to the package we’re getting there.

We both put in our audiobooks and fly. The scenery is still stunning, and we walk across an absolutely gorgeous section of trail. I realize that this is one of the last times I’ll be cruising along in an incredible place, trying to make it to a gas station in time to get a cold drink. This is likely going to be my last resupply on the entire trail. I take out my headphones (Dungeon Crawler Carl isn’t really appropriate for such a moment) and try to fully appreciate where I am and how far we’ve come.

We dip into the forest and are hiking along the White Pass ski area. We’re making good time, but we’re not fast enough and will likely miss out on showers and laundry. This is a bummer, since we haven’t done real laundry since my birthday and haven’t taken a shower in Washington yet. I dig through old FarOut comments and find an alternate people used to take down the road through the ski area. It’ll get us right to the Cracker Barrel, and maybe save us just enough time. We scurry along the shortcut and to the road. Pounding away on a gravel surface always hurts my feet but we’re both hopeful and push the pace. We make it to the gas station just in time; they tell us laundry is closing in 10 minutes. It’s quick work to throw in everything we have besides our rain jackets and sleeping pants. We shower, get our box, and choose a dinner from our re-supply. We have far too much food to justify buying anything.

The hiker area behind the gas station is busy and social. We charge our things and add more than a few items to the hiker box. Most people are taking their time heading north, hoping the fires will go out and the trail will re-open. We are not so optimistic and have family meeting us in Snoqualmie Pass in 4 days. Our plan is to hike there and in all likelihood, conclude our thru hike at that point. Its sad, and we’re more than a little downtrodden. Our bodies are tired though. Sarah has been experiencing an achilles issue that is getting worse and worse. She limps to our camp that night. I roll my ankle on the road and join her in limping. We talk about the possibility of continuing the trail from Snoqualmie, but at this point the alternates do not look good to us. We want to hike the PCT, and with this section in our backyard that opportunity will be available to us another year. We cozy up in the tent and vow to make the best of our final days on trail.

#8256. Everest and Ama Dablam Climbs Resume Despite Cyclone

The second cyclone to hit Nepal’s mountains this season caused heavy snowfall last weekend, but its briefer stay has affected climbers and trekkers less. As the sun returned this afternoon, fresh snow hampered smaller teams on 6,000m and 7,000m peaks, but the highly supported expeditions on Ama Dablam are proceeding with barely a hitch.

No cyclone seems enough to deter the Russian team on Everest for very long. Leader Andrei Vasiliev told us yesterday from Kathmandu that he, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov will return to the mountain in one or two days. The trio is well aware of the challenge they face on Everest’s West Ridge, completely alone and without oxygen.

The climbers’ latest foray up Everest’s West Ridge route. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

Vasiliev mentioned he is under some pressure due to unidentified “unsolved matters” but still determined to tackle the climb. In his own words:

We know what needs to be done; the path is clear, and we must attempt to follow it. We’ve fallen ill. A massive amount of snow has fallen. You adapt quickly to new conditions. Once we’re back in the snow, the cold, and the cramped tent, it will feel as though things were never any other way.

The new snow dump has thwarted some teams attempting Baruntse (7,129m) in the Khumbu. Jan McManus of Ireland was among them, and he has called off his expedition after failing to reach Camp 1 due to deep snow:

It is unclear whether other climbers on the peak may still be trying. There were six large teams totaling 65 foreign climbers with permits for Baruntse.

On Himlung (7,126m), teams hurried to summit and get down and safely away before the cyclone hit. During the previous snowstorm at the end of September, a massive avalanche buried Base Camp, killing 16 staff members. Despite the tragedy, one of the deadliest in Nepal’s mountaineering history, the peak remained open, and guided teams came in large numbers to the mountain a couple of weeks after the accident. A total of 130 foreigners had permits. Teams summited on October 25 and 26, and then left the area.

Ama Dablam Base Camp is also covered in snow, but the commercial teams will nevertheless resume climbing soon. According to Jana Schneider of Germany, climbing with 14 Peaks Expeditions, a Sherpa team is on its way to reopen those sections where fresh snow has buried the ropes. “If all goes well, my summit push begins Nov 4 until Nov 6,” she wrote.

So far, 410 foreigners have applied for a permit to climb Ama Dablam. A Sherpa team first fixed the route on October 17, and dozens have summited since then. Despite the break forced by bad weather over the weekend, summits should continue throughout November.

One climber has perished on the mountain so far, and there have been some close calls. Paul Clarke of Australia and Xenia Santha of Hungary climbed Ama Dablam after attempting Dhaulagiri earlier this season. Their summit push was delayed as they found a 25-year-old climber in a serious situation at Camp 2. Santha and Clarke, who climbed without Sherpa support, gave the climber dexamethasone, spent the night with him, and helped organize an emergency airlift for the following morning. They continued to the summit one day later.

A high camp on Ama Dablam. Photo: Xenia Shanta

#8253. PCT Week 19: Choose Your Own Adventure

📍 Pratt River Backcountry Campsite | 🥾 37.71 km | ⛰️ +902m / -1,527m

This morning we got vortexed. It really wasn’t our fault. We did laundry, and it took forever. When it was finally done we trekked back into the village, picking up a few last minute resupply items from the store and gas station.

Then it was time to head off on a new kind of adventure. The next 70 miles of trail from here were closed thanks to nearby wildfires. But the PCT Association had published an alternate route we could take using other trails. There was a problem, though. Our navigation app was showing that there was a fire on the alternate. We called the Forest Service to check, and they didn’t seem to have any reliable information about it. Deciding we’d rather not accidentally end up doing an out-and-back, we instead mapped out an alternate route to the alternate.

It began with a road walk. Thankfully, it was a pretty quiet road in terms of traffic. The trail proper began with a climb. It was well maintained, and a decent grade – not too steep. But I was dragging. I just couldn’t make my feet move fast, and the group soon got ahead of me. I didn’t mind too much, I knew I’d run across them eventually. The climb ended, but there was no time to enjoy the elevation: the trail sent me straight down the other side of the mountain.

I arrived at a beautiful lake, where the group had decided to take a lunch break and a swim. It was too chilly for me by far, so I just filled up on water and chatted to them for a little while. We agreed on a campsite, and I set off knowing they’d all catch me soon enough.

I twisted and turned down what felt like an endless series of switchbacks through a dark forest, and soon enough the group had overtaken me. But I caught up to them again at a river crossing. I was dismayed to see there was no chance of rockhopping: I hate having wet feet, so shoes off it was. When I got to the other side Shakedown reported that he’d tried to balance on a log, but it had broken into bits beneath him and he was soaked.

From there, there were more water crossings although thankfully none that required shoe removal – they were small enough, or had good bridges or rock hops. The trail from there was through more dark forest, this time lined with ferns that reminded me of hiking in New Zealand. But even though the going was pretty easy, our paces weren’t very high for some reason. Darkness rapidly approached, and we were still miles from camp. The headlamps came out for the last hour of the day, and it grew pretty chilly.

📍 Mile 2,467.4 | 🥾 47.83 km | ⛰️ +1,302m / -1,313m

This morning we had two choices: ford the river, close to our campsite; or hike three miles up to a bridge. I chose the bridge, as did everyone except Catch. He missed out: the bridge ended up being pretty epic, arching above the clear blue waters of the Pratt River. We met up with him at the campground on the other side, then headed down the road for a few miles until we found a picnic table where Shakedown, Sabretooth and I had a late breakfast.

Then it was more road walking up to the next trailhead, where we ran into a large hiking group. They asked where we were heading and when we said “Canada”, looked confused. Normally we get quite excited reactions when we say that, but to be fair this trail isn’t where the PCT usually goes.

The next few miles were nice and flat, and passed by quickly. Everyone got ahead of me again, and I battled up the climb to Snoqualmie Lake alone. I ran into Sass, Sabretooth and Shakedown shortly afterwards at Bear Lake, where we luxuriated in the sun for a little while before hitting the trail once more.

I took my time on the descent to Dorothy Lake. The trail didn’t get much sun, and a lot of it was reinforced with rocks that were slippery with moss. When I arrived at the lakeshore I thought the going would get faster, but it didn’t. Boulders were everywhere, keeping my progress slow. But at the end of it I arrived at a dirt road, and from there I was flying. Soon I’d overtaken Sass, then Sabretooth and Shakedown – who’d all passed me at Dorothy. Not Catch, though. None of us had seen him in a while, so we assumed he’d raced ahead to town.

Towards the end of the road everything began to hurt, and my speed dropped once more, especially when we hit asphalt. The others caught up to me easily as I hobbled through the last mile. Arriving at the highway that would lead us to the trail town of Skykomish, we were dismayed to see a tunnel. We didn’t want to risk walking through it on a busy road, so instead started trying for a hitch. Luckily, we didn’t have to wait long.

We were dropped in front of the only place still serving food past 7pm: the Whistling Post Saloon. We headed inside and began hunting for a table. A local came up, asked if we were PCT hikers, and insisted on buying us a drink when we confirmed we were. Meanwhile, Sabretooth had made friends with some other locals, who invited us to join their table since there were no others free. Then we were offered a free campsite on a local business’s property, and showers at another local’s house. What was going on?? There was SO MUCH trail magic here, it was incredible. “I love this town,” Shakedown kept repeating as we gratefully accepted all the offers.

📍 Mile 2,485.8 | 🥾 30.62 km | ⛰️ +1,361m / -1,119m

By 9.01am we’d grabbed a table at Cascadia and were helping ourselves to huge plates of fried eggs, bacon, fresh fruit and other breakfast goodies. Surprisingly, it didn’t take long for us to eat our fill. Though we did all at least go for seconds, and in some cases thirds. Then it was time to resupply. Our only options were a deli and a gas station; the town didn’t have a supermarket. The locals had all individually been warning us how disgusting the gas station was, so I was pretty nervous about venturing inside. But it turned out to be perfectly fine, and I’d soon picked up everything I needed for the next couple of days.

Getting back to trail required a little bit of tetris in the back of a small hatchback. I climbed in the boot with most of the packs, and the other four all squeezed into the middle seat with a pack or two on top. We were dropped at Stevens Pass which was chock full of cars for a mountain biking event and, we’d soon discover, plenty of day hikers. It felt good to be back on the PCT proper. The trail felt nice and gentle even as it steadily climbed away from Stevens Pass past a series of lakes. We stopped for a late lunch at Lake Janus, where both Shakedown and Sass confessed that when they’d arrived at the lake they’d thought Catch, with his shoulder-length hair, taking a swim in the lake, had been a topless woman. Sabretooth and I cackled.

The afternoon was spent climbing up to Grizzly Peak. I spent most of it doing mental maths. We’d checked the weather in town and seen that rain, and potentially snow, was forecast in a few days. Considering how cold it’s getting, I’d rather be nice and dry in town if it rains. What we hadn’t checked, though, was the forecast at the terminus. I played through potential scenarios in my head, trying to optimise our time on trail.

At the top of Grizzly Peak I ran into three other PCT hikers, and had a brief chat with them. They were planning to cowboy camp up there. Mad respect, it was way too cold in my opinion. After a few minutes I continued on and was met with the kind of view only the PCT provides. The brown ribbon of trail was lined with scarlet bushes, leading me to a wide open meadow of long, faded yellow grass with views of tall pines framing snow-capped peaks in the far distance.

I arrived at the junction to Pear Lake, and found Sass sitting on a rock looking morose. “What’s up?” I asked. He just pointed to the ground near my feet. I was instantly on alert – was it a snake?! No, it was a huge arrow that someone had drawn in the dirt. Sass thought Catch had drawn it, to let us know he’d pushed on past the lake. We discussed what to do. I was pretty set on staying at the lake – I didn’t want to night hike. We decided to wait a little while for Shakedown and Sabretooth. But after only 5 minutes of waiting and with daylight rapidly fading I gave up and headed down to the lake. Sass scuffed at the ground to get rid of the arrow, drawing a new one towards the lake for Shakedown and Sabretooth before following me. But when I made it down to the campsites I couldn’t help but crow with laughter. Catch was there, tent already pitched and dinner well underway. He hadn’t even seen the arrow. Sass’s jaw dropped when he arrived, and we laughed again as we told the story to Shakedown and Sabretooth who arrived not long afterwards.

📍 North Fork Sauk Trailhead | 🥾 48.03 km | ⛰️ +1,593m / -2,467m

By 7am we were trickling out of camp one-by-one, into a beautiful morning full of blue skies and golden sunlight that danced on the changing leaves. Then, after about an hour of twisting and turning through the forest, I arrived on a wide open hillside. It was carpeted in bushes whose leaves were turning vermillion and amber, contrasting beautifully with the proud green trees which pointed towards tall glacier-topped mountains in the distance. It was perfect. Today was the kind of day that leaves you feeling truly awe-struck. It was not a day for listening to audiobooks – sorry, book club. Every sense needed to be available to take it all in. I was practically floating.

At Lake Sally Ann I came across a large group of hunters. A couple of them were pretty chatty, and wanted to know if I was hiking the PCT. They seemed nice, but I was cautious: “Yeah, I am. I’m with a couple of people – you might’ve already seen two of them?” They had. They asked me a few questions about the trail and how to prepare, then admitted they thought they were too old to attempt a thru-hike. “Not at all! There are people in their 80s doing this,” I told them. They seemed intrigued, like maybe they would actually look into giving it a go. I hope they do.

I continued on, making very slow progress as I made the most of the scenery, stopping frequently not just for photos, but to take it all in and commit it to memory. At the border of Glacier Peaks Wilderness I reached a milestone: 2,500 miles on the redline. Wow. Even though I’d had to skip some miles thanks to closures, since I’d tacked on the Tahoe Rim Trail and other side quests I was still well above that number in terms of miles completed while on the PCT. Arriving there alone was a little anticlimactic, though. I’d hoped Catch and Sass would’ve stopped for lunch. They hadn’t, but I decided to stop anyway and enjoy, hoping Shakedown and Sabretooth would turn up while I ate. They didn’t, so after half an hour I pushed on.

A few miles later I came across Catch and Sass lying in a meadow with a spectacular view of Glacier Peak. I threw my pack down and joined them for a little while, savoring this last little stretch of official PCT miles before we once again had to take an alternate – this time, around the Miner’s and Sisi fires. After today’s scenery, being forced to take this alternate hurt. Emotionally and literally. We descended the North Fork Sauk Trail along a series of sharp switchbacks which were filled with golf ball sized stones. By the end of it, my knees were protesting loudly. Thankfully, from there it was flat trail through a gorgeous forest to the campground at the trailhead.

Over dinner, we discussed tactics. Rain was meant to start on day 134. But we were facing around 70 miles of road walking around to the Cascade Pass trailhead, via the town of Darrington. We had no service, so couldn’t check for an updated forecast, but agreed that if rain was still coming in then we’d skip the road from Darrington to the trailhead. We thought it would be pretty pointless to waste lovely, sunny weather road walking on an alternate when we could spend the sunny weather on trail and arrive in town just as the rain started.

📍 Johannesburg Campground | 🥾 28.78 km | ⛰️ +168m / -604m

Although all of today would be road walking, the five of us set out together, spirits high. We walked in a line straight across the dirt road, chatting happily, darting over to the side any time a car approached. Thankfully, they were few and far between. The scenery wasn’t much to write home about, with tall, dark forest on all sides, but the road helped us make good time. We were hitting over 3 miles an hour without even trying.

A few hours in, we found a couple of bars of phone service and checked the forecast. No change: rain was still meant to start on day 134. That was it, then; we’d try and hitch this afternoon from Darrington up to the Cascade Pass trailhead.

Eventually the road changed from dirt to asphalt. It didn’t take long for my body to complain. My feet and knees ached, and I struggled to keep pace with the group. Then it hit me: if we’re already skipping the road from Darrington onwards, why don’t we just skip this road, too? Everyone agreed, and the next time I heard a car coming I turned around and stuck out my thumb. It didn’t take us long to get hitches, and soon we were seated for lunch at Moe’s Cafe, where I demolished one of the best sandwiches I’ve had in a long while. Then we resupplied at the supermarket next door before splitting up to try and hitch to the trailhead.

Catch, Sass and I got our first ride from the first car that passed us, up to the casino on the edge of town. Then the casino courtesy bus immediately offered to drive us as far as the town of Concrete. Win! We were dropped off outside an old gas station. But our luck seemed to have run out. Cars streamed past for half an hour. We moved down towards an intersection, hoping to catch someone coming from another direction. And soon enough we were in yet another hitch. And maybe our luck hadn’t run out after all: he ended up picking up Sabretooth and Shakedown when we drove past them in Marblemount as well, and then he agreed to take us all the way to the trailhead, even though he hadn’t been heading that way. What a legend. Not to mention, he had two very friendly dogs who we enjoyed petting for the entire ride.

We arrived at the trailhead just after the sun disappeared behind the mountains. There was an outrageously beautiful view of the sheer, jagged peaks and their long, shimmering glaciers in the dying light. Unfortunately, the campsite was amongst the trees, so we didn’t get to enjoy it for long. And when we got to the campsite, we discovered that space was very limited. Shakedown and Sabretooth took one spot for their massive 2P Durston, while Catch, Sass and I decided to cowboy camp in the only other spot. There was no way all our tents would fit, and it was surprisingly warm beneath the trees. It felt right to squeeze in a final cowboy on the PCT, too.

📍 Dan’s Camp | 🥾 43.32 km | ⛰️ +1,577m / -1,510m

I’d had a brainwave yesterday. Since we now had an extra day up our sleeves thanks to skipping the roadwalk, why not add on a side quest? My side quest of choice was the Rainbow Lake Trail down to Stehekin, which is a PCT town with a very famous bakery. I’d been a little sad about having to miss it thanks to the fires, but now it looked like I could have the best of both worlds if I did a couple of big days. I couldn’t convince the rest of the group to join me, though. They liked the sound of two shorter days better. So I set off on trail first, and alone. We’d meet up again in Mazama the day after tomorrow.

I was soon speeding past day hikers, and keeping well ahead of a pair of trail runners, feeling very satisfied with myself as I ascended a series of switchbacks up to Cascade Pass. The views up there were showstopping. I was up amongst the peaks we’d admired from the trailhead yesterday afternoon, enjoying the autumn colours that spilled over the landscape below. I was accompanied by a fat chipmunk who had no fear of me whatsoever as he sat atop a stone bench at the pass, clearly preparing for a big day of crumb stealing. The descent, however, was full of rocks, and so it was slower than I’d have liked. But at least there were plenty of gorgeous views of the valley to keep me occupied.

Then I was in the valley, back into the tunnel of trees. I suppose it’s not accurate to call it a green tunnel anymore; there was plenty of yellow, orange and red as well. I paused for lunch at a campsite, and not long afterwards ran into Sass, who’d gotten ahead of me. He told me he was waiting out a bear. Although I’d seen some bear scat on the trail earlier, I didn’t believe him and kept moving forward. He seemed committed, though, and it was several minutes before I heard him steadily gaining on me. Eventually he overtook, and not long afterwards stopped in his tracks, claiming the bear was back. I walked up to where he was, and was a little surprised to see a large, dark brown rear end meandering up the trail. Sass tried yelling “hey bear”, although you couldn’t really call it a yell. I could barely hear him and I was right behind him. So instead we sat down on nearby rocks and waited for the bear to move on.

When we got going again, there was no sign of the bear. Not even any more scat, so we assumed he’d left the trail. Soon afterwards we were rejoining the PCT. This time, though, it didn’t feel so great to be back on the redline. We’d been spoiled by the beauty of Cascade Pass, and now we were just tramping through forest, catching only small glimpses of mountaintops through the canopy.

After only 7 miles, though, we were leaving the PCT once again. Sass had decided to join my side quest to Stehekin after all. We arrived at camp just as night fell, pitching our tents and gathering water in pitch black.

📍 Mile 2,589.4 | 🥾 52.58 km | ⛰️ +2,647m / -2,706m

I’d done the maths, and my Stehekin side quest was meant to be 24 miles, plus another 5 miles to Rainy Pass once we rejoined the redline. Easy. We set off at 7am into a very chilly morning. Our campsite had been down in a valley and the cold air seemed to have pooled there. We wound beneath the treetops, trying to warm up. Unfortunately, the sun didn’t seem to be on our side. As far as we could see, the sky was grey and overcast.

We emerged from the trees into a meadow at the base of a horseshoe of scree-covered mountainsides. We approached and began to climb what turned out to be an excellent trail with fantastic views of the mountains. The wind didn’t let us linger at the top of the pass for too long, though.

We descended quickly, overlooking the namesake Rainbow Lake. What we saw from above made the short side-trip to the lakeshore mandatory. When we arrived we gazed, entranced, for several minutes. The lake’s surface was a perfect mirror, reflecting the scree-filled mountains on its far side that also boasted a collage of autumn colours. When we finally got going again, we congratulated ourselves on making excellent choices.

We continued our descent, catching glimpses of what we thought was a cloud inversion in the valley ahead. As the day progressed the blue sky disappeared, but the cloud inversion stayed where it was. Then we caught a whiff of it and realised we were idiots: it was smoke haze from the Sisi fire. The blanket of it thickened as we descended further and further down the valley, eventually becoming strong enough to scratch at my throat a little. We ended up walking through an old burn scar, too; the combination of it and the smoke was a little sobering.

We made it to the road into Stehekin and started charging towards the bakery. We stepped inside and up to the counter, and my eyes almost popped. The pastries were HUGE, and so cheap. After some deliberation I decided to try the sticky bun, and grabbed a coffee to help wash it down.

After two hours enjoying the comfort of the bakery, we grabbed some cinnamon rolls to pack out for the group and set out on trail once more. It began with backtracking over some of the trail we’d used to get to town, but after a few miles we took the McAlester Trail which would rejoin the PCT seven miles ahead of where we’d left it. It was nice to be able to enjoy some new scenery.

But I was growing tired, and ready for camp. I began compulsively checking Gaia, trying to work out how much further I had to go. It should only have been just over 11 miles from Stehekin back to the PCT, according to my maths. I’d used the official distance from a North Cascades National Parks map and everything! But then I realised: I’d miscalculated. The map showed the distances between campsites, and I’d added those together. But the distances didn’t always appear on the same side of the trail line, and I’d missed a 5 mile section when I was doing the maths. Damn. It looked like it’d be a long night.

We timed it perfectly, though, arriving at McAlester Pass just as dusk began to fall, and entering treeline once more as it grew dark. We walked for an hour or so in the dark until we finally made it to camp, where we set up and ate dinner quickly, exhausted after a mammoth day of mileage and our biggest-ever day of elevation gain.

#8251. One Dead, Two Injured as Two Helicopters Crash Near Everest Base Camp

An Indian passenger died and two more were injured when two helicopters crashed while landing near Everest Base Camp this morning.

The helicopters were operated by Fishtail Air and Air Dynasty, two of Nepal’s largest companies. The crash occurred at the helipad on the outskirts of the village of Pheriche (4,371m). It’s a typical spot for helicopters to stop and refuel when on their way to and from Everest Base Camp.

As shown in the horrific video below, the two helicopters came from different directions, and both tried to land at the same time. Somehow their rotor blades collided. The inexplicable crash occurred in a wide, flat area with good visibility.

Vasanth Kumar, an Indian trekker, died on the spot, The Tourism Times reported. Shailesh Kishan from New Zealand and Rabindra Prajapati, a senior captain, were seriously injured. Both have been airlifted to hospitals in Kathmandu. They were all on board the Fishtail Air helicopter. The Air Dynasty chopper was carrying cargo.

#8248. New Route Attempt on Lunag Ri Falls Just Short of Summit

Between October 23 and 27, Alexander Parfenov and Alexander Semenov of Russia opened a demanding new route on 6,895m Lunag Ri in the Rolwaling Himal on the Nepal-Tibet border. They turned back short of the summit, which some sources list as 6,907m.

The pair climbed a previously unexplored southeast-facing buttress of the Lunag Ri massif. The line would have ended on the southeast summit. It involved mixed and rock climbing to M6, aid sections of A2–A3, ice up to WI5–WI6 in places, and long stretches of steep snow with limited protection.

They placed a piton on the final part of the pillar and began rappelling from there, reaching the base of the wall on October 28, according to gore-ljudje.net. The duo turned back short of the summit due to a coming storm and health issues. The complex summit area — multiple closely linked peaks and ridge features — also left some uncertainty about how close they came to the main summit.

Even without summiting, this was a significant exploration of a major, unclimbed feature on a remote peak.

The new line opened by the Parfenov and Semenov. Photo: Alexander Parfenov

Lunag Ri, the highest peak in the Lunag massif, has long stood as one of Nepal’s highest unclimbed summits. Early attention focused on the broader massif after Joe Puryear and David Gottlieb made the first ascent of the neighboring 6,778m Jobo Rinjang via its South Face in 2009.

In the same year, a Swiss-led team under Stephane Schaffter attempted lines in the area, including approaches to Lunag I, though their claims about summits on the massif were later met with skepticism in the American Alpine Journal.

In the autumn of 2010, a French team that included Max Belleville, Mathieu Detrie, Mathieu Maynadier, and Sebastien Ratel climbed the southeast face of Lunag Ri. Their route, Close the Door (1,200 m, IV/5 F5), was completed in a three-day alpine-style push with two bivouacs. They reached a distinct southeast top (6,812m to 6,830m) on the long ridge connecting Lunag I to Jobo Rinjang. By this time, they were exhausted and did not continue the short remaining traverse to the higher main summit. This remains the only major completed route on the Lunag I massif before the first ascent of the true summit.

From the recent climb on Lunag Ri. Photo: Alexander Parfenov

Attention then shifted to the west ridge and southwest face of the main peak. In November 2015, Conrad Anker and David Lama’s alpine-style attempt reached a high point roughly 300m below the summit before retreating due to the unexpected complexity of the ridge.

They returned in 2016 to try a similar line. On the first day, at about 5,800m, Anker suffered a heart attack and was evacuated by helicopter. Lama subsequently continued alone on a variation that moved farther right onto an icefield. He established two bivouacs and pushed 50m higher than the previous year’s high point before turning around 250m shy of the summit.

In late October 2018, Lama returned solo. Over three days (October 23-25), with two bivouacs, he climbed the southwest face and northwest/west ridge (1,500m of vertical gain, terrain to 90°). He moved mostly ropeless, with limited self-belaying on the harder mixed sections. Lama negotiated the previously unclimbed headwall and made the final exposed traverse onto the main summit.

This was the first ascent of Lunag Ri’s highest point. He descended largely by rappelling down the line of ascent. Lama was awarded a Piolet d’Or for this solo first ascent of Lunag Ri.

From the recent climb on Lunag Ri. Photo: Alexander Parfenov

#8245. The Stairway To Heaven

After a crummy day yesterday I hope to enjoy today a bit more. I attempt to catch another sunset, have I used up all my sunset luck?

Gosh, yesterday’s post was tough. I need a solid bounce-back day. I am not sure how to force that, but polishing off the last of my cold brew coffee can’t be a bad start. I did at least have the excitement of entering a new state, New Jersey, today. I hoped that it would be less rocky than New York. The rocks covered in leafs had proven an unexpectedly formidable opponent. Here I thought I was in the clear once I finished the Whites…not so much it seems.

I headed southbound down the trail from Route 17A moments after sunrise, which is about 11:30AM this time of year. Well, not  really, but it feels crummy being on trail with the sun barely above the horizon only to find that it is already almost 8:00AM. The sun is increasingly not on my side, especially as I planned to take advantage of the flatter terrain and hike over 25 miles.

Shortly after starting out I passed a sign showing the distance to Georgia and Maine. It also advised hikers to “choose happiness”. I don’t know exactly how to do that, but I put on a smile anyway. Anything to avoid having another day like yesterday. In truth, I was over yesterday and feeling good, the extra caffeine had perked me up. After about 2 miles of calm trail, the trail climbed up to a rocky ridge which it followed for the next 4 miles. Looking East from the rocks was Greenwood Lake and the town on the shore of the same name. Planes flew over head every few minutes, a consequence of being under a flight path to the NYC airports, no doubt.

The rocky ridge got tougher as I ventured further south. It undulated up and down constantly and the rock was often smooth, which had the effect of turning my trail running shoes into trail skis. At this point I could feel my left ankle hadn’t bounced back from being twisted yesterday as well as I had hoped. It isn’t a serious problem, a bit like a bruise, but it makes me quite apprehensive when descending a section that doesn’t offer a solid landing spot for my left foot. I took it easy on the descents, but not easy enough. Yep, I ended up turning my ankle again, triggering a pang of pain in the same spot. Again, it wasn’t serious and didn’t slow me down, but these experience sure are getting old at this point.

I believe the light up there is known as “the sun”.

View from the trail above Greenwood Lake.

I had several nice views from the ridge, which eventually reaches the New Jersey border. The trail turns up the state line and, after a few last minute rock scrambles, mercifully smooths out. The next few miles passed through a relatively remote area without much to see but trees. Eventually I came to a trailhead with a clear view north to the town of New Milford.

Another few miles later I came to an enormous pile of rocks with a sign at the top pointing to a blue blaze trail to the Pinwheels vista. It turned out to be a viewpoint popular with day hikers. Far in the distance was a stone tower than I learned marked the high point in New Jersey. The AT passes just past the high point, so I’ll need to make a note to stop by. I took a few photos from the rocky outcrop and moved on to a seriously steep and rocky section of the trail known as the “Stairway to Heaven”. I found it to be as beautiful as it was treacherous. A valiant effort was made to build steps in the hillside, but the leaves had made them slippery. It was fortunate that the section of trail was popular, which did mean many of the leaves were kicked off the rocks. I was taking it slow, but, understandably, I was still quicker than most of the day hikers. I reassured several hikers that, having hiked most of the Appalachian Trail, they were tackling some very difficult terrain. A pair of hikers spoke to me on their way up. When I told them I was hiking the trail twice this year, one could only respond “Wowza!” I haven’t heard that in quite a while!

Rocks, or “ankle testers”, as I have come to refer to them.

The NYC skyline is just visible from the trail above Greenwood Lake.

One of many dirt roads the AT crosses in this remote stretch.

After descending the Stairway to Heaven the trail spends several miles traversing a marshy area, quite a bit of it on a boardwalk. The reeds stretched out a short distance from the trail and offered a different scene from recent days. At the end of the boardwalk the trail climbs up, eventually crossing over Pochuck Mountain. A rocky outcrop provided a great view to the west. My original plan for the day was to hike a few more miles south before turning around and camping at the Pochuck Mountain Shelter. This viewpoint was only another 0.8 miles north, so I could camp here since there was plenty of flat space. The only question was whether I could make it back in time for sunset.

Looking back up the rocks and Pinwheels Vista.

Crossing through the marsh on a boardwalk.

A bridge over a river in the marshy area.

Crossing through the marsh on a boardwalk.

A tortoise takes a break from hiking to drink some water and sit on a log.

Crossing through the marsh on a boardwalk.

I balanced a cautious but expedient descent from Pochuck Mountain, crossing back into another wetland section. I hiked double time on the flat trail, reaching Carnegie Road after 5:00PM. A resident allows hikers to fill up their water bottles at their house, which was clutch as I tried to make time back to the rocky outcrop. I continued retracing my steps, increasing my pace until I looked like I’d lost my mind. I took big steps up Pochuck Mountain with time running out. I could see that clouds were moving in far in the distance. Sunset would either be epic or a washout.

Well, it was the latter. It turns out the sun was a little too far south. If it had been more to the west it would have been setting between clouds, and much more visible from the viewpoint. I had been on a hot streak with sunsets lately so I guess I was due for a dud. It happens. At least I had had a good day, and had a much shorter trip back to the van tomorrow.

Passing the viewpoint for the first time. The tower you can see on the highest hill marks the New Jersey high point.

#8244. Floating Alone Down the Brahmaputra on a Bamboo Raft

Indian mountaineer and adventurer Shekhar Bordoloi has just started a solo expedition down the Brahmaputra River. He set off on a homemade on a bamboo raft from the Dhola–Sadiya Bridge on November 1 and aims to finish at Dhubri, 891km later. The route covers the entire Brahmaputra within India and should take 22 to 25 days in all. The river begins in Tibet and continues beyond India into Bangladesh, covering 2,900km in all.

This won’t be Bordoloi’s first time down the river. In 2020, he and two friends took a similar bamboo raft down a 400km section of the Brahmaputra. Earlier, in 2015, Bordoloi was one of 11 who tackled another part of the river over 11 days under the auspices of the Assam Mountaineering Association. This expedition, however, will test his endurance, pitting him against river conditions for longer, and with less support, than ever before.

Bordoloi on a previous raft expedition on the Brahmaputra. This raft took Bordoloi and friends from the world’s largest river island, Umananda, to its smallest, Majuli. Photo: Shekhar Bordoloi/Instagram

Bordoloi’s raft was hand-built from bamboo poles carefully lashed together over several days. Such craft are a traditional way of navigating rivers across the region, and are still used by local communities for fishing and transportation.

Though the river can be temperamental, Bordoloi’s first two days have been relatively calm, taking him down the Lohit, one of the Brahmaputra’s many tributaries and channels. Navigating the complex river system alone will be a challenge. The Brahmaputra is one of the largest river systems in India, the ninth-largest in the world by discharge, and is prone to flooding and powerful currents.

But according to Bordoloi, those obscure, winding corridors are at the heart of this project. Many sections of the river remain underexplored, and he believes there is hidden potential for the people in his home region of Assam. If he can map routes for river tourism and model environmentally responsible river navigation through those routes, he hopes to draw attention to this important riverine ecosystem and the economic opportunities for the people living along it.

The logistical challenges of a long expedition will further complicate progress. On previous expeditions, Bordoloi traveled with minimal supplies or no food at all, relying entirely on foraging and knowledge of the natural landscape. But this adventure will take over twice as long and may put those skills to their limits.

Bordoloi is documenting his daily progress on Facebook and Instagram.

#8239. Details, Video of Jugal II First Ascent

The Spanish team is back in Kathmandu after their first ascent of Jugal II via a highly difficult 2,000m route. Yet, the climbers insist that the best part of the experience was climbing part of the route with Italians Nives Meroi and Romano Benet. Jugal II was Plan B for the Italian pair after flooding washed out access to their primary target, Tilicho Peak in the Annapurna region.

The peak, northeast of Kathmandu on the Nepal-Tibet border, has been a coveted goal since it opened to climbing teams in 2023. In the end, it was the skill and smart strategy of Mikel Zabalza, Ruben Perez, and Mikel Saez de Urabain that put them on the unclimbed 6,518m summit after an alpine-style push via the east-southeast face.

Route topo, including a special mention of Nives Meroi and Romano Benet.

The team said that the greatest technical difficulties came high on the route. “From the upper bivouac, the climb goes on pretty vertical mixed terrain, with sections of poor-quality rock,” Zabalza explained. “It’s sustained M5 with some even harder sections, until 6,450m. Then the rest of the way to the summit follows along a 55˚-60˚snow slope.”

A tough, vertical mixed section. Photo: Mikel Zabalza

They reached the summit on October 29, at 4:00 pm. The weather was clear but very cold, with some evening humidity.

“We made three bivouacs on the route, two on the way up and one more on descent, and all of them were rather precarious,” Mikel Zabalza told ExplorersWeb from Kathmandu. “Luckily, we had a tarp to enlarge them.”

One of the climbers on the summit of Jugal II. Photo: Mikel Zabalza

The Spanish team, all highly experienced alpinists, had been studying the route for months. This was key to their success.

The situation was different for Benet and Meroi of Italy. Since they had not planned to do Jugal II, their approach to the route was more improvisational. They had no previous information about what they would find. To make matters worse, the third member of the team, Tine Cuder of Slovenia, had to abandon the expedition due to health problems.

One of the Spanish team’s bivouacs, with a tiny ledge enlarged by a fabric tarp. Photo: Romano Benet

There was no competition between the two teams, who happily joined forces for the summit push. However, the Spaniards’ strategy proved essential on the highly steep ramps covered with unstable snow.

Nivel Meroi loaded with bivy gear on highly steep mixed ramps on Jugal II. Photo: Romano Benet

“We set off on an adventure, having never seen the mountain before and not knowing what kind of ascent awaited us, but we gave it a try,” Romano Benet reported from Kathmandu. “We decided to turn back to avoid a third bivouac. ”

The two teams joined forces and were in good spirits on the route. Photo: Romano Benet

Benet explained that they lacked the necessary gear (specifically, a tarp like Zabalza’s group) to pitch bivvies “on this type of face, where it’s impossible to carve out a ledge.”

Otherwise, the two groups returned as friends. “Nives and Romano are exceptional people,” Zabalza said.

“We are back from the mountain with new experiences and ideas but, most of all, with three new fantastic friends with whom, hopefully, we will share more adventures in the future,” Romano Benet concluded.

#8237. How To Layer for Shoulder Season Hikes

Shoulder season hiking, while fun, does present a tricky little puzzle. Morning temperatures often hover below freezing, afternoon sun on exposed ridgelines can heat things up quickly, and unexpected winds can drop the feels-like temperature in minutes. Storms also roll in more often, and snow could always be just around the corner.

Mastering the art of layering clothing is one of the most important backpacking skills for staying safe and comfortable as the seasons change. Instead of wearing one thick jacket, a three-layer system allows you to adapt instantly to changing body output and unpredictable mountain weather.

You can hike in almost any conditions, provided you have the proper safety gear and clothing for the trail. Photo via Katie Jackson

The three-layer system is a standard setup for most backpacking trips. It includes a next-to-skin base layer for moisture management, a midlayer for insulation, and an outer shell for rain and wind protection.

In summer, you’ll want to prioritize lightweight layers for sun protection and cooling, while winter calls for thicker, more insulating clothes (and may even adding an extra layer or two to this system). In shoulder season, you need a bit of both: clothes that keep you from overheating on a tough climb but also warm you in chilly or stormy weather.

A note on fabric choice: Building an effective layering system relies on choosing technical fabrics that work together to manage moisture and retain heat. While cotton certainly has its place in the outdoors, shoulder season is not the time for it. Avoid cotton entirely because it absorbs moisture, holds it against your skin, and robs your body of heat through rapid evaporation.

The first of the three layers is your base layer, the layer touching your skin. A three-season base layer’s main job is to manage sweat. As you exert yourself on a climb, your body produces sweat to cool you; but once you stop moving, that dampness can cool you too much, too quickly. The base layer wicks sweat away from the skin to keep you dry.

To do that effectively, choose a more fitted cut for a base layer top. It doesn’t have to be skin-tight, but it shouldn’t be baggy.

Ideal materials include merino wool or synthetic fabrics. Merino wool has some natural odor resistance and retains insulating properties when damp, while synthetics are more affordable and dry exceptionally quickly. The key rule here is to never wear a cotton T-shirt as a base layer.

A synthetic or wool layer under an insulating layer will keep you much more warm and dry. Photo via Katie Jackson

The middle layer, or midlayer, traps the warm air your body generates while still remaining breathable enough to let excess heat or moisture escape. Its primary function is retaining body heat to keep you warm during cooler periods or while you’re taking a break.

Common choices include grid fleece, lightweight synthetic puffy jackets, or breathable active insulation pieces such as Alpha Direct paired with a wind shirt. Ideal materials allow airflow, which helps prevent overheating while moving.

Choose your insulation weight based on expected temperatures and your personal cold tolerance.

As soon as you stop moving to take in a view, you’ll cool down rapidly. Photo via Katie Jackson

The outermost layer shields you from wind, rain, and light snow, protecting that bubble of warmth created by your midlayer. It functions by blocking wind chill and keeping out precipitation.

The best choices are ultralight rain jackets, waterproof hardshells, or windproof softshells, ideally with pit zips to dump excess heat without removing your rain protection. Make sure your shell is roomy enough to comfortably fit over your midlayer without compressing the insulation. Only choose a softshell as your sole outer layer if you are confident of dry weather throughout your trip.

READ NEXT – The Best Rain Jackets for Backpacking

A large part of layering is trying to keep your insulating layer dry. Photo via Katie Jackson

“Be bold, start cold” is one of the hardest pieces of advice to follow, but people say it for a reason. One of the biggest mistakes hikers make during the shoulder season is starting out too warm; once your clothing gets saturated with sweat, staying warm becomes much harder.

You should feel slightly chilly for the first ten to fifteen minutes of hiking. As soon as your muscles warm up and your heart rate climbs, your body generates plenty of heat, and you don’t want to start out too bundled up. If you, like me, can’t stand feeling cold, you can start with extra layers on — just be willing to stop and shed them the moment you start warming up, even if that happens almost immediately after leaving the trailhead.

Always strip a layer before you start sweating rather than after. The moment you stop for a snack, filter water, or take a picture, your body stops generating heat and you’ll want to put your midlayer or puffy jacket back on to trap residual warmth. If you’ve waited too long to strip, those layers may now be damp at a time when your body desperately wants to retain as much heat as possible.

Stop and take off layers before you start sweating. Photo via Katie Jackson

Extremities lose heat rapidly when temperatures drop, so make sure to complete your layering system with some accessories. A lightweight beanie or fleece headband helps regulate heat through your head, which is one of the easiest ways to manage overall body temperature. Wind-resistant liner gloves or lightweight fleece gloves protect your fingers on chilly mornings. Finally, a merino wool or fleece buff blocks cold drafts from slipping down your shirt collar, and you can pull it up over your face if the wind picks up.

It’s not only important to dress appropriately for changing weather, but also to understand why you’re making your choices. As the seasons change and the weather becomes more unpredictable, understanding these core tenets of layering will help you make the best choices for your environment before setting out on the trail.

#8233. Huge Crowds Trek to Everest Base Camp

The image of an endless line of trekkers heading to Everest Base Camp this week seemed like deja vu. Why are conga lines similar to the infamous ones filmed every May on Everest’s Hillary Step, now repeating at the base of the mountain? We asked the local trekking guide who shot the video.

Ngima Sherpa of Osprey Adventure explained that this is not the norm, but the delay caused by Cyclone Anwar, which hit Nepal last weekend, has created a huge backlog.

“Even though there are always a lot of trekkers heading to Everest Base Camp, this kind of traffic is not usual,” Ngima Sherpa explained. “This video was shot on November 1, after three days of continuous snow and rain…During that time, all the trekkers were stuck in Dingboche, which is two trekking stages away from Everest Base Camp.”

When the weather finally cleared, all those trekkers set off for EBC at the same time, causing heavy traffic on the route from Dingboche to Gorakshep.

The recent cyclone is also the reason why the surroundings are so heavily covered in snow. Usually, the entire trail to Everest Base Camp is dry.

The fresh snow on Nepal’s peaks is having consequences for those planning to summit trekking peaks. Conditions on otherwise straightforward snow slopes have become problematic, as climbers sink into deep, heavy snow.

Satori Adventures had to retreat after swimming in snow on the flanks of Mera Peak, in the Khumbu. “Four to five feet of fresh snow made it impossible to move forward above high camp,” leader Furba Sherpa reported.

Ramesh Gurung noted today that he has retreated from an attempt on 6,119m Lobuche East, another popular Khumbu 6000’er. However, Gurung said he will try again with another group soon.

Conditions will change only as the snow transforms under the dimming sun and freezes in the approaching winter temperatures.

On Ama Dablam, Sherpa climbers struggled to reopen the route to Camp 1 on Tuesday but managed to complete it. The route above Camp 1 follows a steep, mixed ridge with less accumulated snow. Several teams are now on their summit rotations and expect to top out in the next few days.

Tenzing Sherpa of Gokyo Namaste Lodge has shared some useful information for trekkers who plan to cross the huge Ngozumpa Glacier between Gokyo and Dragnag. The recent snowfall makes the usual route less safe, and he recommends following local people along an easier route between Longbanga Tso (1st Lake) and Taujung Tso (2nd Lake). See Tenzing’s sketch of the route:

Alternative route between Gokyo Lakes, suggested by Gokyo Tenzing Sherpa.

Tenzing also noted that the route from Thame to Gokyo is open, as the Gokyo Lodge Association cleared and reopened the trail from the Gokyo side yesterday. However, conditions on the glacier may change quickly.

The route across Gokyo is one of the most popular side trips in the Khumbu, for those wanting to enrich their Everest Base Camp trek. The area features stunning scenery, with high mountain lakes, glaciers, and a view of the formidable South Face of Cho Oyu.

#8229. Animal Attack Roundup, Nov. 4

While they predominate the media reports, most animal attack victims are not tourists unwisely attempting to take selfies with wildlife. People who live and work every day among animals are the ones who most often face the consequences.

As expanding populations push human settlements further into wildlife habitat, we can expect to see more conflicts. Here are some recent incidents.

Photo: Wikimedia Commons/Tisha Mukherjee, CC BY-SA 4.0

In Indonesia, 24-year-old Selviana Ambu Kaka was attacked by a crocodile while washing clothes in the Bondo Kodi River. Her fiancé and his sister witnessed a large crocodile emerging from the water, biting Ambu Kaka on the leg, and dragging her into the river. They immediately alerted nearby relatives and authorities, and a search commenced.

The people of Southwest Sumba, the closest town, organized and combed the area with nets. When they found a large crocodile matching witness descriptions, they hauled it onto shore and killed it. The animal measured nearly 4.9 meters long.

Early on the morning of October 24, Ambu Kaka’s remains were found approximately 30m from the attack site. She is one of many such victims in Indonesia, which sees more saltwater crocodile attacks than any other country.

Habitat destruction is largely behind the massive number of human-crocodile conflicts. It’s an understandably hard sell, however, for conservation workers to convince locals that preventing attacks means protecting the perpetrators.

The victim had recently returned from Jakarta to become formally engaged on October 30.

Photo: Wikimedia Commons/ Rohit Gangwal, CC BY-SA 4.0

A 65-year-old farm laborer, Tulsi Rama Sawar, was killed by a leopard in state of Maharashtra, just north of Mumbai, on November 1. The noise of the attack summoned help from the locals. By the time they arrived, the leopard had fled, but Sawar was deceased. Her case comes less than a month after a leopard killed a 52-year-old woman in the same area.

Town residents are demanding immediate government action to capture the animal. If their demands for cage traps and cameras are not granted, locals threaten collective protest. The attacks represent a threat to their lives, but also their livelihoods, as farmers are unable to work the fields out of fear of attack.

Elsewhere, in Uttar Pradesh near the Nepal border, a 45-year-old farmer named Kennu fought off an attacking leopard, sustaining serious injuries. The man was working in a sugarcane field when the predator leaped out from hiding. Kennu fought back, and the animal retreated long enough for him to flee home, where family members brought him to medical care. Forestry officials have urged agricultural workers to avoid working in the fields alone.

Farm workers are not the only leopard victims, however. Early in the morning of November 4, a 15-year-old girl was dragged from her home in the Shahdol district of central India.

Saraswati Singh Gond was sleeping in bed beside her sister on their veranda, which did not have a door. A leopard entered during the night, not even waking her sister. Singh Gond’s body was found approximately 300m from the house. The search for the leopard continues.

Photo: Wikimedia Commons/Shadow Ayush, CC BY-SA 4.0

Leopards are only one of the wildlife threats that rural Indians face. A 55-year-old woman was gathering mushrooms in Utterakand in northern India on October 30 when she was attacked and killed by a wild elephant. Devaki Rana was lifted up and thrown to the ground, her son reported.

The incident occurred in one of India’s elephant corridors, which allow highly endangered Asian elephant herds to move between their fragmented habitats. The corridors are essential to conservation, but also present a concentrated area where attacks are more common.

Another fatal encounter took place in the state of Chhattisgarh in east-central India. A man of between 35 and 40 years of age, traveling by motorcycle with his nephew, came upon an elephant standing in the road. It immediately charged them, killing the uncle, while his nephew managed to hide beneath a parked truck. Eventually, the elephant left, and he was able to escape.

Locals believe that the elephant in question is one known as Kabra Kaan, which they see frequently and which has been connected with earlier incidents. The Forestry Department, however, has not confirmed this.

Elephant corridors allow them to pass between the remaining forested areas. Photo: Wildlife Trust of India

In Japan, brown bear attacks have been rising for several years. As in many places, human settlements are encroaching on brown bear territory. A decrease in farmland has left no boundary between the urban and the forested worlds. The government has responded with controversial bear culls, despite the concerns of conservation workers.

The latest incident is very different from the increasingly common attack stories. Late on the night of October 30, an express train running on Hokkaido’s Soya Line collided with a large brown bear. The body of the bear was trapped under the train, and the wheels derailed.

A brown bear became trapped beneath the wheels of Sarobetsu No 3. Photo: Hokkaido Railway Company

None of the crew or 32 passengers were injured in the crash. However, fearing more bears were in the area, officials kept everyone on the train overnight, until they could be safely extracted the following morning. Company officials have confirmed that this is the first bear-collision derailment in their nearly 40-year history.

#8228. Snow Capped Mountain Views in Arizona

This morning I got up nice and early at our tent site before the sun came up. The wind was pretty bad last night and was whipping our tents around. I managed to sleep just fine though. Once I got up this morning I made coffee and then began breaking down camp. Then we got moving just as the sun was coming up.

The goal for today is basically just to hike as far as we possibly can. I was looking through my food last night to access how much I had left. There are a couple of different options in terms of which road we hitch into to get back to Flagstaff. If we push really hard we could get in tomorrow night. And if we go a little slower or go further we could get in Sunday night. I think even being out for 2 more full days is going to be cutting it close in terms of how much food I have left. I definitely did grab enough from Gorf’s car. Or maybe I’ve just been eating more than I expected to. Resupplying is always one of the hardest things to do on a thru hike in my opinion. I’ve thru hiked nearly 23,000 miles and I still struggle with it regularly. It can be hard to properly predict the kind of appetite you’ll have and also what kinds of foods will be appealing to you.

Our day started with some double track dirt road walking, with Mount Humphreys peaking out in the distance.

Once we got going the trail continued through rolling fields of shrubs and small trees. It reminds me of a Montana prairie at times to be honest. I’m surprised how the Arizona Trail can remind me of so many different places all at once! Some sections remind me of Montana, Idaho, Wyoming, and even Colorado and New Mexico. Our route brought us through the Babbitt ranch passage this morning. I believe we’ll continue on this passage through the ranch property for the next full day at least.

Unfortunately the wind that persisted for the entire day yesterday was still raging on today. It was still only around 20-30 MPH with gusts up to 40 MPH. There are certainly worse environmental and weather conditions that you can deal with on the trail other than wind, but it can still be its own problem. There have been a handful of days on the trail over the years where I encountered wind around 50-60 MPH consistently. That speed of wind can literally push you over at times. I always try to remember those moments when I get bothered by some light, manageable wind.

The miles were nice and easy this morning through this prairie.

As we continued on this morning the trail weaved through wide grasslands with views of Mount Humphreys off in the distance. We’re going to get closer and closer to the mountain over the course of the day until we eventually go right by the base of it. There is a side trail to bag the peak which is around 13,500 feet high. It was absolutely stunning watching the mountain get closer and closer as the morning progressed. The peak got snow in the recent rainstorm, and it looks lovely up there now.

Early on in the morning I had already begun to feel a pretty ravenous hunger coursing through me. I don’t know if it’s because I’m aware of how little food I have, or if it’s just true hiker hunger setting in. Either way, I was starving. I ate a bunch of my snacks and the remaining rations for the whole day were already running low. Every now and then Slide would snack on something and offer me some of it, knowing I really didn’t have much. I’ll have plenty to eat to get to the next town safely. But when you’re hungry out here sometimes it is really hard to satisfy with just small snacks and things. I call it a hunger that only town food can solve.

As the morning went on we got closer and closer to the massive mountain in the distance.

Around 10:30AM we went past signs for a wildlife watering station, which is of course our next water source. We’re the wildlife out here now! It was just off the trail and a necessary stop. The next sources all look pretty nasty, and the most appealing next source is a long way ahead. We won’t reach that until sometime this evening around the time it gets dark. The wind was still whipping by the time we arrived so we hid behind some shrubs for a brief reprieve. I appreciate the brief “quiet” as well.

After we left the water source we continued along similar terrain for the next few hours. The trail got a bit more “forested” at times, especially in terms of a desert environment. We even watched a large group of elk which were grazing on a hill above the trail. There was one big bull in the group and they all scattered when they heard us coming from a distance. Elk hunting season just started here and the elk definitely know it. We’ve seen a lot of hunters around.

This puffy plant looks like some sort of milkweed. It looked wonderful dancing in the wind.

For most of the afternoon we were continuing through pastures and grasslands, with Mount Humphreys getting progressively closer. The wind made it comfortable to keep all of my layers on for most of the day. I quite enjoy hiking a bit more bundled up when it’s comfortable to do so. It feels cozy! I can’t believe my Sambob Alpha 90 layers are still going out here on the AZT after all of the miles in them last year. But they sure are. And I’ve been loving the ibex wool air puffy that I’m using out on a longer thru hike for the first time. That thing is really cozy but doesn’t get me too sweaty because of the wool. I’m surprised how much I’ve hiked in it on the AZT. I think I’ve done more hiking in a puffy on this trail than any other!

Later on in the afternoon the trail transitioned a bit from the never-ending grasslands to a taller wheatgrass. Which might not seem like anything too special, but is incredibly beautiful while it blows in the wind. All of the tall grass and wildflowers were dancing around in the heavy wind. That was the one bright side of the wind I suppose. By this time Mount Humphreys and its snow-covered peak were right in front of us as well. Boy, is that mountain massive and stunning. It’s hard to imagine such a large peak in Arizona.

Mount Humphreys much closer in the distance now!

Slide was up ahead of me at one point and stopped off to look at something alongside the trail. It was a horny toed lizard that was absolutely adorable. It stuck around for a while and we got to get really close to it. That was one of the bigger horny toed lizards that I’ve seen.

In the late afternoon the sun actually peaked out from the clouds for the first time all day. I was still wearing my Alpha and my puffy and all of a sudden it was scorching out! And just as quickly the clouds rolled back in and I was cold again with fewer layers on. The desert is a wild place.

The trail continued to bless us with great views, large juniper trees, and flowers. As well as those lovely little bridges across the cattle guards. There were some large white plants along the trail which looked like a sort of fluffy milkweed, and those looked fantastic in the blowing wind.

By around 4:30PM the trail had brought us out onto dirt roads. We passed by a bike packer who stopped to chat with us for a minute. He said the upcoming water source was fantastic, which is always nice to hear. But to get to the water source we would have to climb up a particularly steep hill. There was no choice but to climb it. Up top there was a massive trough overflowing with cold, clear water. The recent rain had that thing filled to the brim! As we sat there and the wind blew, water splashed up over the edge of the trough. Slide and I sat there and filled up everything that we would need for the rest of the day, overnight, and tomorrow morning.

Our delicious water source for the evening. It was ice cold and crystal clear thanks to lots of rain.

When we left the water source we got to enjoy going back down that large hill. Then continued along a dirt road for the remainder of the night. By 5PM we had already made it 28 miles, but still had a ways to go for the day. I’m always pleased though when the mileage remaining for the day is less than 10 miles. Somehow 9 miles or less feels very manageable. It’s easy to tell myself that I only have a few more hours of hiking to go.

Before the sun set a jackrabbit ran by us near the trail and we got to watch it scamper off. That was delightful. Those jackrabbits are so fast and hear you coming from a mile away! Then we enjoyed glorious views of the sunset over a field, with Mount Humphreys off in the distance. And a lone cow was out there in the field too in front of the mountain. I thought that made the moment even more beautiful.

This cow looked like it was modeling for calendar or something in front of Mount Humphreys.

My favorite time of day always seems to be when the sun is going down. Watching the sunset is a reward for a long day of hiking. Hiking into the dark is a fair price to pay to get to bear witness to the totality of a glorious sunset. By the time the sun went down I was quite ready to be done for the day. I’d been tired for a while but managed to keep it moving regardless.

Sometime after 7PM I checked my watch and saw we had gone about 36 miles for the day. So we continued along and started looking for a nice flat spot to get set up for the night. We wound up going 36.8 miles before finding a spot and calling it a day. I was tired but felt good! My calves were still sore today, but not any worse than yesterday. They were maybe ever so slightly less sore today. What more could you ask for? After I got my tent set up I made dinner quickly and did my stretching. Then I hardly had any energy left and just called it a night.

I’m a 29 year old thru hiker who has walked over 22,000 miles over the past handful of years. In 2017 I attempted my first thru hike ever, out on the PCT. I completed 1,300~ miles in between semesters of college. Then went back in 2022 and hiked the entire trail over again. The following year in 2023 I hiked the entire 5,600 mile eastern continental trail. Which stretches from Key West, Florida all the way to Newfoundland, Canada. When I completed that trek, I became the 2nd woman in history to hike the entire trail. In 2024 I completed my thru hiking triple crown, after completing the CDT. Then in 2025 I became the 1st woman in history to complete the "border to border" calendar year triple crown. When I finished, I decided to continue hiking for the rest of the year, completing 10,070~ miles in 2025. More miles than any other woman has ever hiked in 1 year and just shy of the men's over-all mileage record as well.
