#8218. How to Skin a Deer Like a Pro

Published Oct 26, 2026 9:38 AM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

If you ask a dozen hunters how to skin a deer, you’ll find that every one of them does something slightly different. While that may be frustrating for newer hunters, it should also be reassuring: There’s no one right way or right order to skin a deer. As long as you follow the general techniques and handy tips outlined below, you’ll be able to skin a deer in no time.

Once you do get the hang of it, skinning a deer is quick and easy. Butchering and packaging a deer can take all afternoon but “if it takes me 10 minutes to skin a deer,” says Cheyne Matzenbacher, a one-time deer processor and current deer outreach specialist for the National Deer Association, “that’s a long time.”

Read through the whole article or click on a topic below to jump ahead.

Although there are lots of tools and setups that can make skinning a deer much easier, the only thing you really need is a sharp knife. The best skinning knives are typically handy enough for maneuvering but durable enough for joint work. There’s nothing wrong with using a small folding skinning knife in the backcountry or a longer filet knife. Just don’t use a dull knife — it’s dangerous and takes longer to finish the job.

Before you can skin your deer, you need to gut or field dress your deer, which involves removing the internal organs from the chest and abdominal cavities. Once your deer is gutted, you’ll ideally want to hang it. It’s certainly possible to skin your deer on the ground or the bed of your pickup (I’ve done both many times), and if you plan to do this, you should study up on the gutless method of skinning deer and other big game. This process is preferred by backcountry hunters who quarter their deer in the field, slip the meat into game bags, and pack it back to camp or their trucks.

But for most whitetail hunters and Western hunters who hunt close to home, it’s easier and faster to skin a deer that’s hanging. The meat will also stay cleaner if it’s hanging instead of touching dirt, bacteria, and deer hair on, say, your tailgate. There are a dozen methods for hanging a deer, and they all depend on your location and the tools available to you.

Deer hunters are divided on this question. You can skin a deer that’s hanging head up or head down, but there are advantages to each method. When Matzenbacher worked as a deer processor for a season, he and his coworkers would hang deer by the head or neck to skin the animal, then flip it to hang head-down for butchering.

“Think about how a deer jumps over a fence: His legs are folded up against his body. Let gravity help you, and let the natural way a deer is going to fold up help you skin it,” says Matzenbacher. “Don’t fight it.”

I skin all my deer head-down, so that’s how I’ll walk you through this example. If you want to try the head-up method, the principles are all the same. Just start at the neck and work your way down. If you are planning to shoulder mount your deer, don’t follow all of these instructions; you’ll need to make very careful cuts near the forelegs and chest. These traditional instructions are for does or for bucks you plan to skull cap or Euro mount. Finally, redneck ingenuity abounds when it comes to skinning deer, and if you’re interested in working smarter, not harder, consider the golf-ball trick or skinning your deer with your truck.

Make identical circular cuts near the knee joints, circling the thin bone of the lower leg on the side closer to the hoof. (This is the only time you should be cutting down on deer hair. For all the rest of the cuts, insert your knife under the hide and cut parallel to the meat or away from the meat.)

Slip the tip of your knife under the hide inside one hind leg. Applying even pressure, cut up and out in a single smooth motion as you run your blade toward the pelvis until you reach the cut you made while field dressing. Do this on the other hind leg, then start to skin the hide away from the tendons where you’re going to put the gambrel and expose the knees. The idea is to remove just enough hide that you don’t have to skin around the metal of the gambrel once you hang the deer.

Thread the gambrel through the natural holes you just exposed in the hind legs (between the bone and thick tendon) and hoist your deer. Tie it off at a comfortable height to work on the hindquarters

Note: You can perform this at almost any point in the process. Some hunters prefer to do this before hanging their deer, others do it as needed throughout the process (as pictured). You can also use loppers or a reciprocating saw for this and may want a saw for the hind legs; just take care not to cut the big tendon on the hind legs.

Slightly bend the front legs and cut through the joint. Wiggle the leg to find the weakest point and use your knife blade to cut perpendicularly through the tendons and between the bones until the joint is free. This may seem tricky at first, but it’s simpler than it looks.

Run your knife between the lower leg cuts and the cut along the abdomen you made while field dressing. Do this on both sides of the inner hindquarters. Combined with the lower leg cuts (or removal) these are the major cuts that will allow you to skin most of your deer.

Using your off hand to lift the hide and your knife hand to make cuts parallel to the meat, begin to peel away the hide. Work from the inside of the hind leg around to the outside. Do this on both sides.

Separate the hide at the tail by either running your knife under the hide and pulling it off the tail like yanking off a sock, or cutting the tail off altogether. Use your knife to work between the joints or simply saw it off.

Now you can begin the easiest part of skinning a deer: letting gravity help you pull the hide off. You may need to raise the deer a little for this part. Once you’ve used your knife to separate the hide from the tail and the inside of the hind legs, set it aside and grab fist-fulls of hide. Using your body weight, pull the hide toward the ground. If the hide doesn’t pull free in places, you can use your knife to help release the hide by slicing the delicate white crackly tissue that connects the skin to the meat. You’ll likely need to do this around the belly area and occasionally along the back

The hide will start to form a tube as you peel it away and it gets closer to the chest and neck.

Before the hide gets in your way too much and starts to drape over the forelegs, make cuts inside the forelegs similar to the ones you made on the hindlegs, starting near the knee joint and running the blade along the backs of the legs until they reach the body and chest. (If you didn’t remove the lower forelegs before, be sure to do this before you try to pull the hide over it.) You can also just pull the skin over the forelegs by pushing down on the hide between the brisket and front of the cut front legs (see video above). It’s similar to pulling off a sock.

Continue to work the hide down over the shoulders and forelegs like you’re peeling off a sweatshirt. The cuts you made on the legs will appear and you can use your knife to free the hide.

Once the hide is over the shoulders, use your knife to separate it from the neck. The freed hide will be heavy now and starting to get in your way. Use its weight to your advantage so it pulls the at the hide still connected to the deer.

When you reach the base of the neck, use a saw or your knife to sever the head from the vertebrae. You’ll have to cut through meat and tendons on all sides until you reach the spine. If you’re using a knife, work through the vertebrae like you did with the knee joints, turning the deer’s head a little bit to help free space between the vertebrae. You want to make your cut at the atlas joint, the connection between the head and the first vertebra of the neck and spinal column.

Once you cut through the neckbone the hide should be completely removed from your deer, though still attached to the head. If you need to get your deer tested for CWD or plan to make a European mount, just slice away all that extra hide hanging off the head.

This step is only necessary if you plan to make your own skull mount. Start at the neck and cut away the skin as you did on the rest of the deer, making cuts parallel to the meat and skull until you’ve removed most of the skin. A flathead screwdriver can help free the hide at the base of a buck’s pedicles, which can be the trickiest part to remove. This is a more time consuming process and should be done carefully to avoid injury or scoring the skull with your knife, which can cause cosmetic damage.

No, you don’t have to hang a deer to skin it. I’ve skinned plenty of deer in the back of a pickup, and sometimes that’s your only option if you’re hunting in areas without many trees or access to a barn or meat pole. It’s definitely easier to skin a deer if it’s hanging since gravity helps remove the hide. It’s also easier to keep the meat clean if your deer is hanging when you skin it; skinning a deer on a level surface like a tailgate or outdoor table makes it more likely that you’ll get deer hair and possibly dirt or bacteria on the meat.

The only tool you must have to skin a deer is a reasonably sharp knife. There are plenty of additional tools that make the job easier, and those will depend on where you’re skinning your deer. If you’re working in the field, consider a hitch hoist for your vehicle and a pair of loppers to quickly remove legs. If you have the luxury of a garage, shed, or barn to hang your deer, along with electricity, you might invest in an electric winch and a Sawzall.

How fast you need to skin a deer depends on a few factors, including the temperature outside and your state’s carcass transportation laws. As a general rule, in the right conditions (cool and dry), a deer can hang hide-on for several weeks. (See below for more details.) If it’s hot and humid, skin the deer as fast as you can to help cool the meat and prevent spoilage. If temperatures are near or below freezing, you should skin a deer while the carcass is still warm and the hide is pliable; skinning a frozen deer is both difficult and time consuming. Meanwhile, CWD laws in your state may require you to debone all deer meat before crossing county or state lines. If such regulations apply where you hunt or live, you’re going to need to skin your deer so you can debone it before you hit the road.

A skinned deer can hang for up to a few weeks if it’s stored in the proper conditions. The deer needs to stay cool and dry, such as sheltered outside during the winter or (preferably) inside a walk-in cooler set to a consistent temperature. Experts recommend hanging deer for 7 to 10 days at a temperature between 35 and 45 degrees to allow enzymes to age, or tenderize, the meat. A deer will not age properly if it’s frozen.

Yes, you can age deer meat with the skin on. Opinions on this vary about which method (aging venison with or without the hide) is better. Any meat that’s exposed to air as it ages will develop a dried crust, and the hide can help protect that meat from drying. I once hung a doe, hide-on, in a walk in-cooler with the temperature set to 38 degrees for two weeks. It was surprisingly easy to skin after aging and I lost less meat than when I age completely skinned quarters. But if you let your deer hang for much longer than that (three weeks or more) the meat may over-tenderize and start to come away with the hide, forcing you to work slowly and possibly wasting meat. Still, letting deer meat hang for at least a day or more can help keep it dry, tenderize the venison, and concentrate flavor before butchering.

The best deer skinning knife is a sharp one. The type of knife—skinning, caping, boning, or filet—matters less than its sharpness and the cuts you make. Many hunters and wild game processors prefer different types of knives for different stages of the skinning process: There are skinning knives (usually slim, handy knives with a sturdy blade), flexible filet knives for working around awkward angles or different muscle groups, caping knives for skinning the shoulders and head of a trophy deer, and stout boning knives for separating knee joints. Try several types of knives to find the best deer skinning knife for you.

Remember, there is no single perfect way to skin a deer. Every deer hunter and processor I’ve met does something slightly different, and most swear their way is the best way. Find which tools and techniques work for how you hunt and what kind of facilities you have access to (if any). The only way to truly learn how to skin a deer is, well, to skin a deer. So sharpen your knife and get after it.

Natalie Krebs is the Executive Editor of Outdoor Life, where she tackles everything from reporting digital features to producing podcast episodes. Originally from Missouri, she currently lives in northwest Arkansas with her bird dog, Hatchet.

#8215. An Old-School Snowshoe Hare Hunt With Hounds Is the Most Underrated Winter Adventure

Published Oct 26, 2026 11:21 AM EDT

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

One of the things I like about snowshoe hare hunting is hot raspberry pie. Few restaurants serve it, especially in the dead of winter in a northern Michigan small-town cafe. One morning last February, my three hunting partners watched with interest, chins resting on their palms, as I sank a fork into the delicacy.

“Do you always eat raspberry pie for breakfast?” wondered Ralph Holsinger, who had invited me to join their hunting group.

“Only when I find a restaurant sensible enough to serve it.”

Another thing I like about hunting snowshoe or varying hares is trying to figure where they will appear ahead of the bawling pack of hounds. It’s a game of constant adjustment—moving up, moving over, squatting low to see through thick cover. You have to take into account the lay of the land and its habitat types and be able to sort out the hound music from what’s hot and what’s not. Sometimes the elastic circles the hares and hounds run are wide, and sometimes they are deceptively narrow.

Playing your hunches is also important because, after all, hares rarely do what they are supposed to do. That’s what Holsinger says, anyway, and he should know: He has been chasing the all-white bunnies for 50 years.

After leaving the restaurant, the four of us took stands along a fire lane through young jack-pine woods that flanked a cedar swamp. In quick succession, two separate hares gave me the slip. The first time I heard the dogs mushing through the snow toward me, I sneaked 20 yards to my left for a better shooting position. But I should have moved 40 yards because when the bounding bigfoot suddenly appeared, it was too far away for a shot. Joe Covert, a member of our hunting party, ended that romp when he shot the hare as it tried to cross the opening. Then, during the second chase, I should have stayed put; this time the elusive hare practically ran over my earlier position, but I wasn’t quick enough for a shot. It slipped by the other hunters, too, and now the pack had driven the snowshoe deep into the swamp.

We waited, 100 yards apart, and shuffled our feet against the cold. Thirty minutes passed, and now it was 10:30. Then I could hear it—the faint squeal of Squeaky, Holsinger’s lead beagle. Soon, Rambo barked in with a coarse bawl. The stretched-to-the-limit circle was tightening once again. The other dogs—Shane, Twinkie, Candy and John—began to cut loose with assorted chops, yelps and squeals that were definitely growing louder. The gutsy pack of hounds was pushing this splayfoot right down my throat. For once, I wouldn’t have to move at all.

Sinking to haunches, I swept the woods slowly from left to right and waited for the hare to materialize. You never hear snowshoe hares, at least not with snow on the ground, and certainly not with the hounds chorus ringing through the woods and in your ears. No, like true ghosts, snowshoes take shape before your eyes. Suddenly, and with a rush of adrenalin, they are there. So where was this one? The dogs were closing in too fast. Already I could see their skinny tails whipping left and right, but no rabbit.

There comes a point when the hunter of hares knows he has failed, and usually that is when he sees the dogs. They filed by at 30 yards, eagerly punching their noses in and out of the loose snow and ignoring me altogether. How did they know I was no threat to any swamp ghosts today? Snow-choked cedars muffled a shotgun blast, which told me that one of the other hunters, probably Marty Anthony, had ended this nonsense. So much for my hunches.

Seven species of hares—which actually differ from rabbits because they are born fully furred and with eyes open—are native to North America. The snowshoe, or so-called varying hare, turns all white in the winter and is the smallest. At an average of 14 to 15 inches, hares are a little longer than cottontail rabbits. At an average weight of 3 1/2 to four pounds, they are a bit heavier, too. Range of the hare includes the northern tier of states and all of Canada and Alaska. They also live in mountainous regions of the Alleghenies, California and New Mexico. Besides Alaska, 20 states have hunting seasons.

In addition to mysterious population swings that affect both rabbits and hares every 10 years or so, snowshoe numbers rise and fall dramatically according to habitat availability. In areas of aggressive timber-cutting activities or where fire has destroyed a forest, hares thrive on the new growth for a few years. Then, when the forest begins to mature, the animals may all but disappear.

According to Ben Tullar, a wildlife biologist with the New York Department of Environmental Conservation, abandoned farms in northern New York first support red spruce, balsam fir and white cedar. These conifer species get a head start on hardwoods such as maples, beech, yellow birch, black cherry and white ash. “For example, after a period of only five to 15 years,” Tullar said, “an abandoned pasture can support a huntable hare population for another five to 15 years. But the hardwoods eventually overtake the conifers, and a hardwood/softwood mixed forest develops with little understory vegetation and, consequently, no food or shelter for hares.”

When the habitat is right, populations explode because few animals are as prolific as snowshoe hares.

Snowshoe hares are an important food source for hawks, owls, foxes and coyotes. Apparently, hunting by man has little impact on their populations, and that is why seasons in most states are long and bag limits are usually liberal. Wisconsin hunters, for example, have enjoyed no closed seasons and no bag limits since 1965. During peak years, though, they shoot only about 3 percent of the state’s hare population. In Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, Oregon and Washington, hares go underharvested most years.

Hares rarely hole up, a habit that makes them available to hunters on all but the coldest days. In bad weather, they crouch under snow-laden branches and have been known to tunnel under snow, but they don’t usually go underground, even when pushed by a hound pack. Most jumped hares don’t seem to be afraid of the dogs anyway, and I suspect that is because they know they can’t be caught. Most of them amble along, taking their time a few yards ahead of the dogs that flounder in deep snow. Put a crust on that snow, though, and hares will pick up enough speed to keep just ahead of the pack. Generally hares run a wide circle, returning to the same vicinity where the dogs started them. But not always. I’ve seen hares lope through the woods for a mile on a course as straight as a Nebraska section road. Years ago, Holsinger was hunting a linear strip of woods, between a Michigan Upper Peninsula highway and Lake Superior, when his dogs jump-started a snowshoe. When the rabbit took his dogs out of hearing, Holsinger leaped into his truck and drove two miles to where the cover petered out. Ten minutes later he shot the animal when it came bounding through. Most hares would have crossed the highway at some point; Holsinger’s hunch that this one would not paid off.

On a warm, sunny afternoon you can post an area punctuated by the Y-shaped prints of snowshoes and sometimes get shots at animals sunning themselves. Stillhunting, tracking and stalking are effective ways to hunt them, too, if you remember to move slowly and bend down to rabbit-eye level now and then. Just as quietly moving deer hunters look for the flick of a tail or some other part of a buck’s anatomy, so, too, should hare hunters watch for telltale movements or black-tipped ears on the white-on-white bunnies.

It’s easy to find out if hares are using an area by keeping an eye out for their tracks, trails, droppings and eating signs. Saplings girdled near the ground are pretty good clues that a hungry hare stopped by. If food is plentiful, snowshoes will occupy a five to 10-acre area all winter. But if food is scarce, they will migrate several miles in search of something to eat.

Sometimes hares can be pushovers but not very often. One occasion is during years when their populations are cycling high and the animals don’t exhibit the same degree of caution they do during lean population years. The other time is when a fluke of nature puts all-white hares in snowless woods, a condition that can happen in the late fall or late winter. Then, the rabbits are as easy to see as the Blaze Orange clothing on your hunting partner. Nature always helps wild things to adapt, however, because in portions of Oregon, Washington and British Columbia, where snow is generally scarce, snowshoe hares don’t turn white at all.

No matter where you find the varying hare, the most exciting way to hunt them is with hounds. Best scenting days are when temperatures are near freezing or higher and the snow packs underfoot. Worst conditions are extreme cold and powdery snow because what scent there is gets easily covered by the first dog floundering on the track.

“Only the hounds seem to know if hunting will be good or not,” said Holsinger, who has owned and raised dozens of high-stamina beagles, which are most hare hunters’ dog of choice. For two years a couple of Holsinger’s friends kept careful records, noting such hunting-day conditions as temperature, humidity, wind and dog behavior. Their conclusion? Not only is every day different, but it is often unpredictable. On good-weather days the dogs sometimes had trouble getting a chase going, and then on certain days of poor conditions, they ran well.

“Just listen to those hounds,” Holsinger said as he and I hurried down a logging road next to a swamp where the dogs were puzzling out a fresh track. “We put a new dog in that pack, and the music is sweeter than ever.”

Holsinger was striding along in front of me in a place where the woods necked down. Bouncing from one side of his game bag was the white head of a hare. Sticking from the other side were the fuzzy feet of another snowshoe. “The dogs are turning this way,” he said, looking back at me. “Where do you want to set up?”

Read Next: A Christmas Hunt for the Black Hare of Halcott Mountain

“I’ll take a stand right here,” I said and waved him on. “I have a hunch the rabbit will cross at this bottleneck.”

It didn’t. Instead, the hare loped across the road in front of Holsinger, who bowled it over with a load of 12-gauge, No. 5 shot.

It just wasn’t my day for hunches, but all was not lost. I knew where to get another wedge of hot raspberry pie.

This story was originally published in the December 1990 issue of Outdoor Life.

#8213. Winter Hiking Boots FAQ

If you plan to hike this winter, buy insulated, waterproof winter hiking boots to protect your feet and keep them warm. Regular hiking boots intended for three-season conditions, mids, or trail runners lack enough insulation and may not stay waterproof in wet snow, puddles, or slush. Even regular leather hiking boots treated with waterproofing products can absorb moisture, becoming cold and potentially freezing during a long outing. This can lead to discomfort, frostnip, or frostbite in severe conditions.

Insulated winter hiking boots are a much better option because they have waterproof construction, rubber or waterproof synthetic lowers, and insulation that helps retain warmth even if moisture enters from above or accumulates from perspiration. While waterproof membranes such as Gore-Tex can reduce water entry, they cannot prevent dampness from sweating or the chilling effect foot perspiration can cause in cold winter weather. When that happens, insulation remains the most important factor. A damp insulated boot can still retain warmth better than an uninsulated boot that has absorbed water and begun to freeze.

When choosing insulated winter hiking boots, you’ll want boots for the temperatures you expect to encounter, usually between -10°F and 35°F, although you may encounter even colder temperatures. People with cold feet may want to get more heavily insulated boots to stay warm. The temperature ratings that winter hiking boots come with assume active use, so it pays to get a boot that is even warmer if you have to stop and stand around for a while. Say, for instance, a companion is injured. You’ll want boots with enough foot insulation to stay with them until help arrives.

Winter boots generally fall into three categories:

Each type is designed for different conditions and activities, from winter hiking and snowshoeing to ice climbing, snowmobiling, and ice fishing. The best choice depends on how much you walk, how cold and wet the conditions are, and whether you need to use traction devices such as microspikes, snowshoes, or crampons.

The waterproof/breathable liners, like Gore-Tex, built into cold-weather boots usually do a good job of keeping moisture out, especially when the boots are new. But it doesn’t hurt to add extra waterproofing, like Sno-Seal, to the outside of the boots, especially along the seams, for added protection. Waterproof/breathable liners do break down with use, and it’s good to have a backup strategy. These liners also provide poor breathability in winter, and your socks will likely get damp from perspiration if you’re active. While not ideal, this is normal, and the added insulation will keep your feet warm.

If you plan to hike or snowshoe in winter, you’ll want insulated, waterproof boots designed primarily for walking, not more technical activities like mountain climbing or ice-climbing, or sedentary activities like snowmobiling or ice fishing.

Winter hiking boots look like regular hiking boots, mid-height boots, or even boots with coverage above the ankle, but they’re all waterproof and insulated. For most winter hiking and snowshoeing, boots that extend just above the ankle are the most comfortable and practical. The more calf coverage you have, the warmer your feet will remain.

Winter hiking boots should have laces instead of slip-on designs or zippers so you can tighten the fit. When walking on snow or ice, lug depth and rubber type matter less than your ability to use traction aids like microspikes or snowshoes, which bite into the surface and keep you from slipping. For instance, anti-slip rubber soles designed to prevent slipping on urban sidewalks are virtually worthless if you need to wear microspikes for traction most of the time.

Synthetic insulated boots are usually lighter and more water-resistant than leather boots. The insulation will be built into the boot and not removable, which keeps the weight down and makes the boots easier to walk in. The amount of insulation you need depends on the temperature, how active you will be, and whether you will walk continuously or stand still for long periods.

Winter boots are commonly offered with 200-gram or 400-gram Thinsulate insulation, although PrimaLoft or Aerogel insulation is also used and provides the same level of warmth retention. The 200g and 400g quantities refer to the insulation’s thickness or density, not its weight inside your boots.

As a general guide, 200-gram insulation suits active use in temperatures around 0 to 10 degrees Fahrenheit, while 400-gram insulation is better suited to temperatures between approximately -20 and -40 degrees Fahrenheit. These estimates assume that you are walking rather than standing around. Individual experiences vary considerably.

We recommend the following insulated 200-gram and 400-gram winter hiking boots:

Regardless of insulation level, check that your boots work properly with your microspikes, snowshoes, or crampons. Traction devices should not create excessive pressure on your toes or the front of your boots, since this can cause discomfort and blisters. This is often the case with lighter-weight winter hiking boots or mids that have soft uppers.

Mountaineering boots are designed for steep, technical terrain and ice climbing. They have rigid soles that support crampons and allow climbers to stand on small edges of ice or rock. They are also generally heavier, less flexible, and less comfortable for ordinary hiking than insulated winter boots. They can also be quite bulky and may not be compatible with microspikes or even snowshoe bindings. Mountaineering boots I recommend.

Mountaineering boots are available in single-layer and double-layer designs. Single-layer boots, like those listed above, are intended primarily for day trips in exposed alpine terrain. Double-layer boots have a removable liner and are best for overnight trips because you can remove a damp liner and sleep with it, preventing it from freezing overnight.  They’ve largely fallen out of use, but if you’re going someplace where you need them, you can often rent them from mountain guides, especially if you’ve hired a guide service.

If you need a full crampon compatible with the flexible soles of insulated winter hiking boots, look for one with a “flexible leaf spring or center bar,” like the Camp Stalker Universal Crampon. This flexible center bar connects the front spikes to the rear spike assembly. The flexible bar prevents the crampon from snapping in half when used with boots that have more flexible soles.

Pac boots usually have a rubber lower section, a leather or synthetic upper, and a removable felt liner. They are designed for very cold, wet conditions, but their warmth comes with several hiking disadvantages. Pac boots are heavy, bulky, extend well above the ankle, and provide limited ankle support.

They suit activities that require little walking, such as ice fishing and snowmobiling.

Their large size can also make it difficult to fit with microspikes, crampons, and most snowshoes. For active winter hiking, insulated hiking boots are usually a better choice.

Boot warmth ratings are useful for comparing products, but they are not standardized. Manufacturers may test their boots differently, and a rating cannot account for every person or condition.

Your experience will depend on factors such as:

Read customer reviews and look for boots that have been sold for several seasons. Recommendations from experienced hikers and people you trust can also be useful.

Beyond insulation and waterproofing, several design details can improve comfort and performance.

A manufacturer’s temperature rating provides a rough indication of warmth, but it should not be treated as a guarantee.

A sturdy toe cap protects your feet and helps prevent the front of the boot from collapsing under tight-fitting microspikes or crampons. A collapsed toe box can cause pressure and blisters.

A gusseted tongue is attached along its sides to the inside of the boot. It helps keep water from entering through the laces when you step into deep snow or puddles.

The cuff is the upper edge of the boot around your lower leg. A soft, comfortable cuff helps retain heat and prevents snow from entering when you walk through deep snow.

Deep, well-spaced lugs provide traction on packed and loose snow. Rubber compounds and tread patterns vary, but a durable sole such as Vibram can provide reliable grip. On ice, you will generally need microspikes or crampons in addition to the boot tread.

A gaiter ring near the toe allows you to attach the front hook of your gaiters. If your boots do not have one, you can often attach gaiters to the laces instead.

Winter boots should not be tight. A cramped boot restricts circulation and can make your feet colder. Your toes should have enough room to move, but your foot should not slide excessively from side to side. Your heel should remain secure when the boot is fully laced.

Try on winter boots with the socks you plan to wear. If you wear thick winter socks, try them on during the fitting process. When between sizes, it is usually safer to choose the larger size. You can fill a small amount of extra space with thicker socks or higher-volume insoles, such as Superfeet. You can’t make a boot that’s too small larger.

#8212. Class 4 Terrain, Cozy Huts, Cold Beer: The Northern Alps Are Japan’s Best-Kept Secret

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Author and photographer Andy Cochrane spent months crafting this route from home in Bend, Oregon, consulting with multiple Japanese mountain guides, before flying to Tokyo to bring it to life. Along with four others, he ran this 100-mile technical traverse across the Northern Alps in a week, staying at mountain huts and soaking in Japanese hospitality along the way.

It’s not often that a local guide recommends helmets for a hut-to-hut trail running trip, but it’s always a sign of a good adventure if you ask me.

A couple of months before flying across the Pacific to Japan, I was on a mid-afternoon Zoom call—my third such conversation of the week—when my jaw hit the floor. I was meeting virtually with guides in the Northern Alps to learn more about the trails and huts of the range, hoping to suss out if a line I had plotted on a map was actually a feasible endeavor to run.

At the time, I wasn’t sure if anyone had run the route before us. There certainly weren’t any blogs, articles, or posts I could find about it. Hut owners on the trip later confirmed my suspicion that our 100-mile, seven-day itinerary was pretty far out of the box. Connecting the outdoor hub of Kamikochi at the southern end of the range to the Sea of Japan in the north along a single ridge line was an unheard of idea to everyone we spoke with. That made it a lot more exciting—and far from certain it would work out. If it did, however, we would get to experience all that the Northern Alps had to offer in a single push.

Because the route required a mix of trail running, boulder hopping, ladder climbing, and Class 4 scrambling, our local guide Tatsuro was adamant that we bring helmets, even if their use wouldn’t be required every day. TL;DR: he was right.

Before I get into specifics of the route and experience, let’s set the scene. The Northern Alps, or Hida Mountains, are Japan’s most primal terrain. Although lesser-known than the mountain ranges of Europe, South America, or mainland Asia, the Northern Alps are just as technical and challenging, if not more so. The range is a jagged, granite spine that defies the country’s reputation for manicured serenity. Trails in the Hida are riddled with boulders, ladders, roots, scrambling, and thick brush. Located just a few dozen miles off the Sea of Japan, the weather is incredibly fickle in the Hida, too.

Geographically, the Northern Alps lie just a few hours drive west of Tokyo on the main island and stretch across Nagano, Toyama, Gifu, and Niigata prefectures. Most of the range is inside Chubu-Sangaku National Park, which protects around 670 square miles from being absorbed by the urban centers that surround it. The Hida are widely regarded as Japan’s premier alpine terrain and feature the country’s most developed hut system, Yamagoya. These staffed huts offer hot meals, sleeping mats, water, snacks, and beer, allowing for multi-day runs and traverses with lightweight packs sans camping gear—perfect for a trip like ours.

Three years ago I ran across the Southern Alps on an ancient postal route called Nakasendo. While the Southern and Northern Alps offer remarkably different terrain and technicality, my first trip taught me much about Japanese culture and logistics that was helpful while preparing for my return.

Perhaps my biggest takeaway from that initial experience was that the language barrier is a major challenge—especially in rural places, where many people don’t speak a lick of English. While apps like Google Translate can help to order a quick meal or get assistance with navigation in a pinch, planning a trip and booking mountain huts requires someone not only fluent in Japanese, but who also understands the mountain culture. For us, that liaison was Kota.

I was connected with Kota at Japan Adventures Co. through a friend, and I honestly can’t say enough good things about him. He is an incredibly organized planner, a great communicator, and an avid hiker and trail runner. He even helped negotiate our stay with a few huts that didn’t believe our route was possible, ensuring the entire trip ran smoothly. Kota and his team lead a variety of hiking, food, and cultural trips around Japan, and are currently rolling out new trail running itineraries in the Northern Alps and elsewhere.

With help from Kota and advice from guides like Tatsuro and Paul from Nagano Adventures, I was able to refine our route to stay at unique huts, run the best trails, and find a balance between challenging and doable for each day. It’s important to note that mountain huts in Japan are warm and welcoming, but they run on rigid schedules. Breakfast is typically at 5 a.m. and dinner is around 5 p.m. If you don’t check in by 4 p.m., they will notify search and rescue, so it’s important to start early and keep an eye on your pace throughout the day.

My goal was to start in Kamikochi and end at the Seas of Japan, creating a single linkup by connecting a number of popular two- and three-day hiking routes—the Panorama Ginza Route, Mount Yari, Ura Ginza Panorama Route, the ridgeline from Mount Eboshi and Funakubo-dake, the Hachimine Kiretto, the Kaerazu no Ken (ridge of no return), and Tsugami Shindo. It’s a mouthful to say, but when drawn on a map, the routes piece together nicely, forming a (mostly) straight line running from north to south.

Getting to and from the Northern Alps isn’t terribly difficult. After landing in Tokyo (either HND or NRT), a bullet train, or Shinkansen, will take you to Matsumoto in just a few hours. From there you can take a smaller train, bus, or taxi into the mountains to begin your adventure. Returning to Tokyo is just as easy by hopping on a bullet train in a coastal city like Toyama. There are plenty of stations to choose from and you usually can find seats just a day or two in advance.

There are a few ways to shuttle your luggage from the start to the finish, but I recommend Yamato Transport. Other options include dropping bags at the post office, the front desk if you’re staying in a hotel, or even convenience stores like Lawson’s or 7-Eleven. Though this might seem risky at face value, it worked flawlessly for us. We walked into a convenience store around 10 p.m., spent a meager ten minutes filling out the paperwork, and walked out. Our bags arrived at our final hotel just after we arrived seven days later.

Despite plenty of challenges, the trip ran as smoothly as I could have imagined. We dealt with heavy rain, 50 mph winds, and thick mist for our first few days, which forced us to slow down on the scrambling sections, layer up to stay warm, and take plenty of breaks in huts along the way. Some days had tons of vert (often more than 1,000 feet per mile) and rocky trails that made running difficult, so we embraced the shuffle. On day four, when covering our most remote section, we didn’t see a single other person. Fortunately the trails are well marked, even where they are less frequented and overgrown.

The crux of the route, the Kaerazu no Ken, is a long and serpentine downclimb on Class 4 granite slabs, offering a chain for protection in some areas while others did not. This was one of the dozen or so sections that having a helmet was a welcomed addition to our kits. For those comfortable with alpine climbing, this will feel like a fun change of pace. For those afraid of exposure, it’ll be challenging. The huts themselves vary considerably from small ridgetop outposts like Funakubo to much larger and busier outfits like Hakuba Sanso. Regardless of size, every hut owner we met was incredibly kind. Japanese hospitality is something they take very seriously.

Overall, our experience in the Hida was more than we could have asked for. Steep and technical trails, unique and cozy huts, fickle yet fruitful weather, and no other Americans or Europeans along the way. It’s an undiscovered gem for anyone outside Japan. With the help of Kota, Tatsuro, and others, I’m already planning a return trip next year.

One of the lightest climbing helmets on the market, the Vapor was perfect for our trip. We frequently had sections of running between scrambles and wouldn’t leave it on because it breathes so well. The Vapor fits over a hat and under a rain jacket hood, making it great for wet days, too.

The latest from Garmin is designed for routes like ours with a solar-powered display that ran the full week on a single charge. The maps were critical on wet days when I didn’t want to use my phone, and the flashlight was perfect for early mornings trying to not wake up other guests.

The perfect size pack for a trip like ours, the Adventure was able to carry everything we needed—spare clothes, first aid, snacks, camera, and ditty—with ease, plus poles, flasks, and a phone in the external pockets. It can be adjusted on the fly to reduce bounce and chafing.

On a week-long trip you end up eating a ton of snacks—gummies, chips, gels, and whatever you can buy at the huts—but nothing hit home like GU stroops. Whether it was with morning tea, on the top of a big climb, or preventing a bonk, stroops played a big role in our success.

With major improvements from the previous version, the Speedgoat 7 was the perfect shoe for this trip, offering plenty of grip on technical scrambles and ladders, a comfortable and cushy ride for the long days, and a lay-flat tongue that kept most rocks and dirt out.

The perfect mid-layer for cool mornings or windy days, the Dawner breathes well and is quite comfortable next to skin. The exterior is stretchy and durable, which is great for running through brush and rubbing against rocks— an inevitability in terrain like the Northern Alps.

#8211. Does This Advanced Method of Scent Control Actually Work for Deer Hunting? Here’s What 5 Independent Testers Had to Say

Published Oct 26, 2026 1:06 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

Many of the deer hunting strategies we rely on aren’t scientifically proven. For the most part, we go with the gear and tactics that have worked in the field, not necessarily in research studies. The most controversial example of this is probably scent control. Numerous products claim to minimize human scent, and some of them are gimmicks. In this world of scent-control, the most technologically-advanced strategy — as well as one of the most dubious — is to use ozone.

Ozonics is the company that first used ozone to minimize hunter’s scent in 2007. In the decades to follow, the company has sold hundreds of thousands of units, says Ozonics president Buddy Piland. The current topline Ozonics unit costs $456 (on sale), which is serious cash for most deer hunters. Piland admits that marketing Ozonics so it’s perceived as a legitimate product (and not a gimmick) has been a challenge over the years.

“I’m selling you an invisible molecule,” he says. “I’m saying ‘Hey, there’s something coming out of this box that will keep deer from smelling you.’”

So is the price of Ozonics worth it? Do these units actually work as advertised?

You can search around on the internet and find testimonials from a variety of deer hunting personalities promising that Ozonics is a “game changer.” But you can also find testimonials from hunting personalities and influencers promising that almost any gear item out there works, no matter how frivolous it might be.

Cynical deer hunters don’t believe the hype, and they might not even believe the anecdotes of outdoor writers and editors. As hard as we searched, we couldn’t find any scientific, peer-reviewed research on the effectiveness of using ozone to kill human scent in the field.

So we devised a totally anecdotal, but also totally unbiased, experiment of our own. We gave new Ozonics units to five diehard deer hunters who have no sponsorships, TV shows, or big social media followings, and had them test the units throughout their 2023 deer season.

They are all experienced and skilled hunters who have killed big bucks over the years, but they’re also regular dudes. Most of them work blue-collar jobs when they’re not hunting. They have no problem calling out bullshit. Most importantly, they spend a lot of time in the woods. Altogether, they had more than 400 deer encounters while running Ozonics units.

We sent each hunter a survey at the end of their season. We did not pay them for participating in the survey (and neither did Ozonics).

But before we can decide if Ozonics works, or doesn’t work, we need to understand ozone. As Piland puts it, ozone is a molecule made of three connected oxygen atoms (O3), which is unstable and wants to revert to its natural state. Ozone attaches to bacteria or scent molecules and oxidizes them. Ozone is used in a variety of industries (you can read all about it here) but the takeaway for deer hunters is that the ozone being created by an Ozonics unit is supposed to attach to our scent molecules and neutralize them, thus preventing deer from smelling us.

There are a variety of ozone-producing devices on the market that can be used to treat clothing (usually in a bag), but Ozonics is the only company that produces a device suitable for use in the field.

Explained very plainly, an Ozonics unit creates ozone by sending high-voltage electricity through a coil and then blowing air across that coil. Over the years, the company has experimented with different levels of ozone generation and modern units now have selectable levels of ozone to match a variety of field conditions.

Piland says the best way to visualize how ozone and scent work is to imagine a stream with rocks and eddies that disrupt and change the flow of water. That’s a lot like how wind works as it moves across the landscape. Now imagine pouring red dye (your scent) into the stream. It won’t flow consistently downstream. In some places it will move faster, in others it will stop and pool. Lastly, imagine dropping purple dye (the ozone) into the stream on top of the red dye. In some places the purple will completely blanket over the red (effectively destroying your scent). In others, the red and purple will blend to make a slightly different color (altering your scent).

“[With ozone] sometimes you’ll see deer and they’ll definitely smell something, but they don’t panic and run away,” Piland says. “It’s more like, ‘Oh, I’ve never smelled that before.’”

And finally, in some places the red dye and the purple dye will never overlap. The same thing can happen with your scent in the wind. The faster the flow of the stream and the more eddies it has, the more purple dye you’ll need in order to obscure or change the red. In the field, this means more wind and more unstable wind means you need more ozone to neutralize your scent.

“So what you need to do [while hunting in higher winds] is figure out how to best dump your ozone … by adjusting the angle of the unit and the distance it is from you,” Piland says.

All our hunters reported that Ozonics either had a “very noticeable positive impact” on their hunt or “some noticeable positive impact” on their hunting. All of them said that they would continue to use Ozonics in the future.

Combined, they had approximately 435 deer encounters and were clearly busted by deer a total of 24 times. That’s a rate of only 5.5 percent, with many of the encounters occurring downwind. Some hunters had zero deer bust them throughout the entire season. Their anecdotes from the field provide examples of how the units performed.

“A good example of the Ozonics helping was an evening hunt in late October. Four doe and fawns came in upwind. A mature buck followed them in about 15 minutes later and started pushing them a little. Three of the does eventually got downwind of me. They definitely noticed a smell they didn’t like, but never were able to get enough scent to spook. They spent 10 to 15 minutes walking around with their noses in the air trying to smell me. Meanwhile the buck spent close to 10 minutes within 20 yards of me making a scrape and just watching the does. I decided not to shoot the buck, because he had a smaller rack, but there is no doubt in my mind that I don’t get that opportunity without the Ozonics.”

“Yes, even when trying to play the wind, deer still often manage to get downwind at times.  I have noticed that with the unit on, their reaction is much less of an issue when they do get downwind. My experience has been that deer either walk right through my scent cone or if they do stop and try to wind me, they are unsure of what they are smelling and eventually continue past without snorting or blowing. The unit is not foolproof but it certainly helps, based on my experiences.”

“We had a questionable to flat-out-wrong wind a few times this season while sitting over food plots. Normally I would hunt something else or stay home in this situation, but I was curious about how well the system would work in this scenario. In one hunt, the deer entered the field, and they fed into my downwind side. The younger deer had zero idea that we were there. An older doe picked up enough to know that something was off, but she couldn’t seem to pinpoint our location or gather enough scent to sound the alarms. She moved about 15 yards, slightly alerted, but was calm and feeding again within a minute.

I was very skeptical before using the system. It’s impossible to completely fool a deer’s nose. However, hunting from the ground and having deer downwind of me on multiple occasions, and not having them blow out of the field in most cases was a bit mind boggling to me. The deer that would detect something seemed to be confused about what, or where, I was. And that definitely bought me more time to make a shot. I killed a nice buck in the bluffs of Minnesota where my wind was swirling fairly bad. He came to 20 yards and didn’t have a clue I was there. I’m fairly certain that scent was pushing up into the ravine at the time he came in, as I could feel the wind shift onto my neck blowing into his direction. Judging from my encounters with hundreds of deer and countless ‘scent destroying’ products, Ozonics was the only one that I believe to work as they advertise, in most cases.”

“I had many encounters with deer coming in downwind, with zero instances resulting in any deer blowing. I did, however, definitely have some encounters where I do believe the deer smelled something — whether it was the ozone or a hint of me.”

“I had deer walk to 10 yards downwind. They knew something was up but never busted.”

The hunters in our survey had a clear-eyed perspective on Ozonics. They all felt that it worked, but no one said that it was a silver bullet for fooling deer. They also agreed it was not a perfect unit — most agreed that it would be better if the unit was quieter. It didn’t spook deer, but it made it harder to hear deer approaching. It’s a bit of a hassle to set up. Plus, there are minor health concerns involved with using ozone. You should make sure to educate yourself on those issues if you’re considering springing for a unit.

But the numbers don’t lie. The hunters in our survey encountered a ton of deer and spooked very few. They all attributed at least some of that success to the Ozonics units working effectively. That might not count as scientific data, but in the mysterious world of scent control, it’s as good of a field test as you’re going to find.

Alex Robinson is Outdoor Life’s editor-in-chief. He oversees an ace team of writers, photographers, and editors who are scattered across the continent and cover everything from backcountry sheep hunting to trail running.

#8208. This Bowhunter Took World Record Bull Elk in Back-to-Back Seasons

Published Oct 26, 2026 4:00 PM EDT

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

This story about bowhunter Jay Elmer was originally published in the November 1981 issue of Outdoor Life.

Many hunters dream of taking a world-record animal, but for most of us it remains just that—a dream. For Jay Elmer, the dream came true—twice!

Taking one record animal may be no big deal. Anyone can get lucky once. But two times? And in consecutive years? That’s what Jay Elmer did. In 1979, hunting with bow and arrow, he killed a bull elk larger than the world record at that time. Before that animal could be recognized officially, Jay returned to the field in 1980 and took an even larger bull.

Lucky? No, he’d planned for those animals and drew on skills from a lifetime of hunting to get them. Maybe the story of Jay Elmer’s two for the record will help you plan for a dream come true.

Hunting has been a way of life for Jay, the oldest of 14 children. At 5 years of age, he began hunting with his dad, but before long he was hunting on his own. First for rabbits and squirrels, then for deer. In the eighth grade Jay bought his first rifle and that year killed a deer with it.

“In high school I didn’t do the things most guys do,” says the soft-spoken Elmer, now 36. “I ran around with guys 10 years older than me. Instead of going to dances and running around town, we were always off hunting.”

Jay grew up near Sedona, Arizona, at the mouth of spectacular Oak Creek Canyon, 30 miles south of Flagstaff. Today he owns a plumbing business in Sedona. Over the years he killed deer, antelope, elk, and bear. For a 10-year period Jay filled almost every tag he got, often with trophy-class animals. As his success grew, hunting seemed to lose some of its zest.

“I still loved to get out, but I had to put the challenge back into it,” Jay said. “So in 1974 I started bowhunting. With a bow you have to get close. It puts a real thrill and challenge into hunting.”

While scouting that first year, two weeks before the season, Jay and his brother Bill saw three large bulls.

“I kind of had my heart set on one of those bulls,” Jay said. “On opening morning I had 13 bulls in one bunch parade right in front of me. But all were spikes and two-points. It was tempting, believe me, but just killing an elk wasn’t all important. So I controlled myself. I wanted one of those big bulls, but I never saw them again.”

Not until his third year of bowhunting did Jay finally score. In 1976 he killed a bull that scored 351, at that time good enough for 11th place in the Pope and Young bowhunting records.

For those unfamiliar with scoring, antler measurements are the basis for record-book placement, and they’re a good way to judge the comparative size of animals in the field. Most hunters will never see a bull that will score 351. The average five-point measures about 200, the average six-point between 250 and 275. Most hunters would consider anything over 300 to be huge. Minimum score to make the Pope and Young archery book is 240. The Boone and Crockett minimum is 375.

From then on, Jay decided, he’d take nothing smaller than his first bull. That meant looking for an area with bigger bulls and fewer hunters. Localities with the most elk don’t necessarily have the biggest bulls. Trophy bulls often stay in isolated pockets where cover and terrain give them the needed protection to grow old.

Jay found such a spot near Flagstaff. At best it was marginal elk country. It looked so bad that no other bowhunters had touched it. The junipers and jack pine were thick enough to choke a snake. It was dry and hot. During his first year of scouting there in 1976, Jay didn’t see one elk. The second year he scouted and hunted the whole season and saw a single cow.

But he stuck with it. He wasn’t after just any elk. He wanted a big one, and based on sign, he knew at least one lived there. Big tracks told him that, but Jay looks for something else, too.

“A big bull’s front hooves are larger than the rear hooves,” he claims. “As the animal walks along, you can see the rear tracks outlined inside the front tracks. I don’t know why the front hooves are bigger. Maybe a trophy bull needs extra support for his heavy rack.”

Rubs, where this particular bull had shredded trees with his antlers, also impressed Jay.

“I held my arms straight over my head, and the rubs still reached several feet above my fingertips,” Jay said, his voice quivering with excitement. Jay is about six feet tall, so he can reach close to eight feet high.

“Then there was the pine branch three inches in diameter and ten feet long. It was lying thirty yards from the nearest pine tree. You just know it took one tremendous bull to tear it off and throw it that far.”

Finally, late in the first day of the 16-day season in 1978, Jay saw his first bull in the new area. He had a good shot at the giant animal, but his arrow glanced off a branch “just as a bullet might.”

Still Jay didn’t give up. In such dry country elk use water holes, so he checked some of them for tracks and built blinds and stands at those he thought the bull was using. One day a five-point bull ran right under his tree stand and stopped nearby to bugle. Jay didn’t shoot. He eventually spent the entire season hunting the bull he’d shot at, but he never saw it again.

On opening morning of the next season Jay and his wife Cheryl took stands at a water hole. Bulls bugled on a nearby ridge for half an hour before a six-point ran from the trees behind Cheryl and into the water. She shot, but the bowstring hit her sleeve and her arrow splashed into the pond. The bull fled.

Then a bull that Jay thought would score 350 came within 30 yards of his stand. Another bull almost as big walked by no more than 30 feet away and waded into the water. Most hunters wouldn’t have hesitated, but Jay was determined to hold out for an elk larger than his first. He decided to give Cheryl a crack at them. He heaved a baseball-size rock into the water hole. The bull stood belly deep, looking straight up. Jay stifled a laugh and threw another rock. This time the bull was up to his ribs in water, staring skyward. The other elk stood on the bank.

Finally Jay got so frustrated that he stood and waved his arms. The bulls trotted by Cheryl but she missed.

After that Jay started hunting a long ridge not far away. On the fifth day of the season he saw a big bull. He spent the next three days working on that animal, trying stalk after stalk, but he couldn’t get close enough for the shot he wanted.

Unlike most bowhunters Jay does little calling. He listens for bugling bulls and then stalks them. This way, he thinks, he can hunt a particular bull for a long period without spooking him. He wears camouflage clothing and smears his face and hands with black camouflage paste to be as inconspicuous as possible.

He tries to anticipate the elk’s route and to put himself in the animal’s path. That’s when knowing the lay of the land pays off. Jay studies maps before the season, looking for water sources and landforms; then he drives every road and trail to get intimate knowledge of the country and to look for elk crossings. To avoid spooking animals, he does little walking before the season. He tries to discern patterns the elk follow, particularly where they water and bed, and which routes they follow. With this background he often can plan a stalk to ambush a moving bull. If he starts a stalk and can see it’s not perfect, he backs off.

“You arrive at a point when you have to decide if it’s a good stalk or not,” Jay says. “If it’s not, get out of there and try another approach. Once you rile a bull, odds are he’s going to be twice as hard the next time. I may try several stalks in a single morning.”

Jay hunts only early and late, when elk are moving on their own and can be seen more easily. He doesn’t want to be in the woods when animals are bedded, because he thinks his chances of shooting a bedded elk are zero. And he thinks it’s a disaster to rouse a bull from its bed.

On the evening of the eighth day of the 1979 season, Jay found the trail of three elk. Then he heard a bull grunt. Thick scrub oaks and jack pines blocked his view, but he judged the animal to be 500 yards away. He slowly moved toward it. About halfway there he glimpsed brown and chocolate elk hair moving through the trees toward him. Jay stepped into a shadow. As the animal came within 40 yards, walking fast and steadily, Jay could see this was the bull he’d been working on for the past three days.

He nocked an arrow, but it caught on his bowsight and clattered across the pins. The bull jerked his head up and stared, straining to see through the screen of shadowy branches. Then, strangely, the bull walked toward Jay. At 25 yards, he tore into a little oak tree with his antlers. The elk turned, started into a small opening, saw Jay, and turned toward him. Jay slowly pulled the string back, aimed, and released his arrow. The bull whirled and crashed away. Jay waited a few minutes, then started trailing carefully. He found the bull dead, about 400 yards away.

The bull officially scored 384⅝, four inches larger than Doug Kittredge’s world record.

One world-record elk should be enough for any hunter, but Jay Elmer wasn’t finished. Last year he returned to the same place. No one but his friends had hunted there, and he knew big bulls still lived there. On his fourth day of hunting he found some tracks, which he thought were made by 15 to 20 cows and five bulls. That afternoon he and Cheryl took stands there. Thirty minutes later a herd of elk crashed through the jungle of limbs and brush. A seven-point bull brought up the rear about 70 yards from Jay. He guessed it might score close to 400.

The next day Jay got an early start. He loves to hunt with his wife, but this time they both knew that wouldn’t work. This was his bull. Nothing was said. Jay just slipped away quietly into the black forest alone.

By sunup Jay had caught up with the animals. Three of the bulls were calling back and forth. He followed them about a mile and sneaked within 50 yards in thick junipers, but he could see only legs. Four times he started to stalk in for the shot, and four times he backed off. The last thing he wanted to do was to shoot prematurely. He would accept only a close-range, sure-kill shot. To get that, he had to make a perfect stalk.

After his fourth try, the time was 8:30. Getting late. The elk would bed soon. Jay knew he had only one more try. While scouting he’d seen where elk had traveled into a ravine. He decided these animals would go there, so he circled ahead and stood behind two pine trees 30 yards to the side of the ravine.

Twenty minutes later a dozen cows and calves walked within 25 yards. The wind was right and they couldn’t catch his scent. The big bull that he wanted came within 50 yards, but Jay could see only the polished-ivory tips of the great antlers.

For five minutes the cows and calves milled around Jay. Then a lone cow walked directly behind him and stopped 15 feet away. Jay felt helpless. He couldn’t move. Moments later a large six-point bull emerged from the dense trees to the side and strolled to the nearest cow. Apparently the bull Jay wanted saw this and decided to run off this interloper. The antlers, and then the massive body, appeared over the mound. The bull walked rapidly toward Jay—40 yards, 30, then 20. Jay drew his bow. The bull froze, facing head on. His head was down, covering most of his chest. Waiting for the animal to turn broadside, Jay began to quiver. The 78-pound bow would wait no longer. With the 20-yard sight pin just under the bull’s nose, Jay released the string. The arrow hit dead center in the chest. The elk crashed away for 50 yards, smashing logs and trees in his path. Then he plowed into the ground like a crashing airplane.

Read Next: The Real Story Behind the Casey Brooks Bull, the Pending World Record Elk

Not until he walked up to this great animal and saw clearly the size of the antlers with the seven beautiful polished-ivory tips on each side did Jay feel nervous. His knees began to shake. He knew he’d outdone even himself.

Because Pope and Young records are updated only every two years, Jay’s 1979 bull would never be recognized as a world record. The magnificent animal at the hunter’s feet now was even bigger. It measured 389⅝.

Jay Elmer’s bulls now hold the No. 1 and 2 spots in the Pope and Young record book. Could one hunter ask for more? Knowing Jay Elmer, I figure he’ll be going for a bigger one this year.

#8206. ATN Thor 6 First Look: The One and Done Thermal Scope?

Published Oct 26, 2026 5:56 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

There is a dizzying array of thermal scopes on the market, and finding the right one for you typically starts with deciding how you’ll use it. Are you hunting hogs over bait? Or calling in predators in open country?

Those two use cases are on either end of the thermal scope spectrum. You really don’t need to spend $10,000 on a scope with a 1280 sensor for close-range hog hunting. A 640 or even 384 optic with a lower base magnification is plenty for that job. On the other hand, David Stroud, a serious competition predator hunter, once told me, “The best is barely good enough,” for his use case.

But, after testing the ATN Thor 6 -LRF, I found it’s a scope that can do just about anything. It’s not completely overgunned — or overpriced — for hog hunting, and the 640 variant is plenty capable for predator hunting. The added LRF, ballistic calculator, and easy controls make it a solid all-around optic. Here’s what I think of it after initial testing and a detailed comparison of the 13 different Thor 6 models.

The Thor 6 LRF has a 1,000-meter rangefinder built into the scope. There’s a dedicated ranging button that’s easy to find in the dark. If you have the ballistic calculator set up, the adjusted aiming point will automatically appear. This system makes shooting at night much easier because you have zero depth perception through a night optic.

The Thor 6 has the form factor of a traditional scope, which makes it easier to use in the pitch dark. Instead of a series of buttons, you have a combination of knobs and buttons for your critical adjustments. The focus control is where you’ll typically find the parallax knob on a traditional scope. You’ll navigate the menu using the elevation turret. The zoom and ocular focus controls are in the same spot as a standard scope. The buttons to start recording video and range targets are large and easy to reach.

One of the hardest parts of getting a thermal scope into the field is figuring out the menus, zeroing it, and just figuring out how the thing works. I’ve tested dozens of thermals and I still get tripped up by some optics. ATN saves you from thumbing through the owner’s manual and watching YouTube tutorials to figure out your new scope. There’s a built-in AI assistant within the ATN app. You can ask it any questions you have, and it will give you the answers. The app is also where you can review your video recordings, stream a live view, and adjust settings.

Thermal scopes are expensive and they have delicate sensors that can be damaged by sunlight. One of the easiest ways to damage your scope is to leave the objective lens uncovered in direct sunlight. ATN helps you mitigate that by outfitting the scope with a lens cap that’s actually quite good and a neoprene cover. They’re nice accessories to have straight out of the box.

Much is made of a thermal scope’s resolution and image quality. But, I think the big differentiator is the user experience. I want a scope that’s easy to zero, easy to adjust, and that I can use while blindfolded. Fumbling around in the dark for the focus or burning a box of ammo to get zeroed are the experiences I avoid like a coyote with mange.

So I was relieved that the ATN Thor 6 was easy to mount and get zeroed. I set one of the included thermal targets at 50 yards and opened up the zeroing setting. Then I fired a shot and checked its location with a spotting scope. Next, I adjusted the zero by moving the reticle from my aim point to the impact location. It’s a simple process, and you can even freeze the image to make it more precise. My next shot was within a few inches of my aim point, and after a small adjustment, I was dead on with my third shot. I moved the target to 100 yards to get my final zero, which required only two shots. So with five shots, I had the scope zeroed and the chronograph data I needed to set up the ballistic calculator.

After zeroing and setting up the ballistic calculator, I started shooting targets at various ranges. The ballistic calculator worked as I expected, with first round impacts at all distances. I’ve had some scopes that refresh constantly and seriously disrupt your ability to scan for animals. The Thor 6 has long a period between refreshes, which I appreciated. After shooting this scope on the range, I can’t say enough good things about how easy the menu is to navigate and how intuitive the controls are.

I’ve spent the last few years falling down the thermal optics rabbit hole, doing everything from an annual trip to Texas to test the latest in night optics to managing predators on my lease. While I’ve tested a ton of different optics, the one constant has been a Horizon Firearms rifle in .22 Creedmoor. The Horizon rifles are unquestionably accurate, handy, light, and the best turnkey coyote gun I’ve used. My current rifle is a Vandal 2 with an 18-inch barrel and chambered in .22 Creed. It shoots 80-grain Hornady ELD Match at 3,018 fps and easily maintains sub-MOA accuracy. The bare rifle weighs around 7 pounds, which is light enough to be handy but still heavy enough for stability. On the muzzle end, I added a Dead Air Nomad Ti OTB, which is an over-the-barrel suppressor. Its design keeps the gun short because only half the suppressor extends beyond the muzzle. The ATN Thor 6 rounds out the build nicely because it’s a truly versatile optic.

Scott Einsmann is Outdoor Life’s gear editor. He oversees the gear team’s editors and writers who are subject matter experts in bows, knives, hunting, fishing, backpacking, and more. He lives in Richmond, Virginia with his wife and two bird dogs.
