#8121. The World’s Most Cinematic Trail Running Is Hidden Above the Arctic Circle

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Trail Runner’s travel columnist Andy Cochrane has run all over the world, including five trips to the Lofoten Islands above the Arctic Circle in Norway. He shares his hard-earned recommendations on where to run, stay, and eat, what to pack for the unpredictable weather—and how to get there.

As a travel writer, I fly an embarrassing amount. Over three quarters of a million miles in the last decade, or roughly three laps around the Earth each year. That’s a lot of time in a pressurized tube sitting next to strangers, but perhaps a fair price to pay for the privilege of running trails all over the world, from Patagonia to Morocco to Greenland. Picking a favorite destination is difficult, but often actions speak louder than words. I’ve returned to one more than any other: the Lofoten Islands in Norway.

Hidden a hundred miles above the Arctic Circle, Lofoten is best known for its Viking heritage, red fishing  villages, and dramatic coastline—sandy beaches, turquoise waters, and walls of rock that rise 3,000 feet out of the Norwegian Sea. There are very few places in the world where mountains collide with the ocean in such a cinematic way, giving it the best of both worlds—and incredibly unpredictable weather.

On my first trip to the Lofoten Islands in 2017, a snow storm shut down trails in the alpine, so I explored the lowlands, dabbled in fishing and kayaking, and enjoyed a nightly sauna. Since then I’ve returned four times to explore different corners of the islands and am planning to go back again next year, because there is still so much to explore, especially if you love empty trails and technical running. Here’s why I think Lofoten could be the next great trail destination and how you can visit before it gets too crowded.

The Lofoten Islands are an archipelago in northern Norway that stretch from the mainland into the North Atlantic. At 68 degrees 54 minutes north latitude, they sit further north than most communities in Greenland and all but a dozen or so towns at the top of Alaska. The chain consists of five main islands and hundreds of smaller ones, connected by bridges and underwater tunnels. (Oh, the joys of Norwegian infrastructure!)

Combined, the islands cover a total of 474 square miles, roughly the size of the city of Los Angeles. However, they are home to just 25,000 full-time residents, most of whom live in Svolvær and Leknes. Suffice to say, the interior is remote and rugged; it’s common to find yourself on a trail without a single human in sight, despite the lack of trees and views in all directions.

Although there are offshore oil reserves nearby, drilling is prohibited in Lofoten (unlike much of Norway), which has allowed cod fishing and tourism to flourish. The landscape is a mix of granite spines and tussocked tundra, with a few birch and mountain ash stands sprinkled in. When storms roll in—which they do often—there is very little protection, which can be a humbling experience.

The trail network in Lofoten is a patchwork of everything from unmaintained user trails to heavily engineered routes like Reinebringen’s 1,978 stone steps. As a whole they skew towards the technical end of the spectrum; most are steep, rocky, and stout. It’s common to gain a thousand feet per mile or more.

The vast majority of trails start near sea level and ascend through bogs and brush, climbing into the alpine via scree fields and off-camber granite slabs. Expect your shoes to get muddy and shirt to be saturated in sweat as you climb to the summit. Some marshes have wooden planks and some ridgelines have cairns, but they aren’t guaranteed. It’s best to always bring a good map and a better attitude.

While there isn’t an official count of trails on the islands, a good estimate is around 150, including everything from short beach hikes to high ridge lines. For ambitious trail runners, the Lofoten Crossing is an unofficial 100-mile thru-route from Delp to Å, and uses a mix of local paths, beaches, and roads. It’s a great way to see the entire chain of islands, even if it skips some of the serene trails. A few of my other favorites are the steep climb up to Himmeltindan (2,700 feet in 2.1 miles), crossing the interior of Vestvågøya from Leknes to the eastern end, and almost any of the remote trails at the end of the archipelago near Å, many of which reside inside Lofotodeen National Park.

Lofoten sees over a million tourists each year, heavily focused on the summer months. The crowds get so bad in July and August that iconic trails like Ryten, Fløya, and Mannen are probably not worth visiting. In the spring and fall Lofoten becomes a lot more enjoyable, because it offers more solitude on the trails, open spots at restaurants, and generally friendlier locals. I have a slight preference for the fall, mostly because I reserve most of the spring for skiing, which also is pretty great in Lofoten.

It’s also worth considering the weather and daylight. For about a month from early December to early January, the sun doesn’t rise above the horizon. Days lengthen dramatically in the spring, from 6 hours in February to over 18 by the end of April. The Midnight sun rises in late May and sets in mid-July, offering 24 hours of daylight for a month and a half straight. Almost too much!

Weather is fickle all year but especially in the spring and fall, as temps float in the 40s and 50s Fahrenheit. Snow usually melts in May and the mountains undergo a rapid transition to green. In the fall the foliage turns to a golden and red mix, storms begin to batter the coast, and the Northern Lights illuminate the night sky as early as September. Thankfully saunas are common and help make cold weather running more enjoyable.

Getting to Lofoten takes more time than most destinations in Europe. The drive from Oslo is around 20 hours and the combination of train and ferry takes even longer. The fastest way to get to the islands is a flight to Bodø and then a puddle hop prop plane to Svolvær or Leknes. This saves time and helps avoid weather-dependent ferries, but is often more expensive.

I prefer to fly from Oslo to Narvik, which sits on the mainland adjacent to the islands, and rent a car. The drive takes between 2-4 hours, depending on where I’m staying, but is always worth it for the views. Plus, public transit is limited in Lofoten, so having a car allows me to get to quieter places. For example, the cinnamon rolls at Unstad are to die for—but the only way to get there is to drive (or go on a 80-mile round-trip bike ride).

Traditional fishing lodges, called rorbuer, are built on poles over the water. Many have been converted to cozy places to stay. My favorite is Hattvika Lodge in the town of Ballstad. The restaurant next door, Fangst, is one of the best in the area. For those wanting to stay further off the beaten path, Nusfjord would be a great option. For a wider selection of restaurants, consider a stay in Svolvær or Leknes. Regardless, it’s important to book early, because the best places fill up months in advance.

If someone told me the Offtrail Ultra was designed specifically for Lofoten, I wouldn’t blink an eye. The 5 mm lugs are perfect in mud and scree, the toe grip is great on granite slaps, the integrated gaiter keeps out debris, and the midsole is stable enough for the dynamic movements necessary in this terrain. Hard to imagine a better fit, honestly.

Designed for cold and wet weather, the Run Cold wool socks are designed with high-impact wear zones to help them last longer, but don’t feel overbuilt at all. Instead they are stretchy and comfortable, with a seamless toe to reduce chafing. They work well with tights and running pants, which I use in spring and fall running in cold climates like Lofoten.

Over the last few years I’ve trended towards running belts, but I make an exception for a place like Lofoten, where you want to bring a few extra things. The Triack has a snug fit with almost no bounce thanks to a bungee system that’s easy to adjust on the fly. Plus, with four easy-access pockets, I can carry spare layers, gloves, snacks, water, camera, and first aid easily.

The name is a bit of a misnomer, because it’s actually made of merino wool. The wool helps regulate temperature better than other materials, keeping you warmer at the start and cooler when you heat up, not to mention not smelling after days of use. I love the hood and neck gaiter for colder days, and how the hoodie works great under a raincoat, too.

#8120. The 10 Best Snowboard Boots of 2027

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

What to know: After testing 38 pairs of snowboard boots, our crew’s favorite all-mountain options are the Nitro Team Double BOA (men’s) and the ThirtyTwo Lashed Double BOA (women’s). If you’re looking for a comfortable, more affordable pick, it’s hard to beat the Nidecker Altai, which is available in men’s and women’s sizes. Heading into the backcountry? Check out the versatile ThirtyTwo Focus BOA x Sweetin or the skintrack-slaying K2 Waive.

Testing snowboards is one of our favorite things in the world. Testing snowboard boots? Not so much. Quite frankly, it’s hard to find a pair of snowboard boots that fit your anatomy and riding style (not to mention budget), and breaking in a new pair can be daunting even for seasoned snowboarders.

Luckily for you, our crew of diehard testers risked blisters and toe bang while putting 38 pairs to the test in the Rockies, Wasatch, and Sierra over the past couple seasons to bring you the best snowboard boots available today. Below, you’ll find our top picks for boarders on a budget, tried-and-true favorites for all-mountain riding, as well as powerful freeride boots and our go-to option for splitboarding.

Pros and Cons + Versatile for true all-mountain use + Comfy out of the box + Solid heel hold – Hard-chargers may crave a stiffer freeride boot – Fit can be snug

Nitro’s best-selling Team is an all-mountain menace that’s dependable from park to peak. This double BOA version pairs new H5 BOA coilers with Nitro’s fast-and-easy inner lace system, which kept our ankles locked in place for responsive turns and smooth transitions.

The main draw of the comfy-out-of-the-box Team is its versatility. A Tahoe tester who loves throwing down in spring parks as much as he does exploring Palisades hike-to terrain found the mid-stiff Nitro supplied the sweet spot of support and shock absorption. There’s enough lateral give for jib laps and tweaked airs, and the molded backstay provides stability on steeper descents. Meanwhile, the EVA foam liner, EVA midsole, and an airbag pocket in the heel make for velvety-smooth landings. Plus, the Vibram outsole was at home scrambling in the alpine. “Zooming around on melted rocks was totally chill,” reported that Tahoe tester.

These Nitro boots are best for intermediates and up, but heavier, hard-chargers may gravitate toward a stiffer boot in serious freeride terrain. Fit was on the snug side, so it’s smart to size up a half size. It also comes in a wide version.

Pros and Cons + Comfy out of the box + Lightweight + Good shock absorption – Flimsy insoles – Durability concerns around the foam outsole – Doesn’t pair with FASE bindings

The lightweight, affordable, and medium-flexing Nidecker Altai also happened to be one of the top rated snowboard boots in the comfort department. An Eastern Sierra tester with a history of foot pain was impressed by the coziness from lap one. “I haven’t had these professionally fit, and they are remarkably comfortable out of the box,” she reported, shouting out the plush, foot-hugging liner and the roominess of the 3D-molded toe box.

After replacing the “flimsy” stock insoles with custom footbeds, a snowboard instructor called the Altai “perfect for everyday riding” thanks to “a blend of comfort and responsive mid-flex.” She co-signed the double-BOA lacing and Velcro-cuffed liner that stayed tight and secure. The asymmetrical closure, which shifts BOA lacing inwards and over the flattest zone of the forefoot, is a hallmark of Nidecker boots, and the Swiss outfitter claims it reduces pressure and discomfort. Testers confirmed as much: “Stayed tight, no pressure points, super comfy,” said one.

By loosening the upper BOA, a freestyle-oriented rider could dip in and out of the park, boning tweaked grabs and buttering to his heart’s content. The lightweight, cushy foam outsole absorbed flat landings well, he reported, although multiple testers worried about the foam sole’s durability compared to harder-wearing rubber outsoles found on the pricier options in this guide. Additional dings? The lipped backstay doesn’t fit well with FASE bindings while unstrapping, and a couple of testers had to size up a half size.

Beyond that, our crew recommended the boot for lower intermediates to advanced riders, warning that newbies could benefit from a softer flex and hard-charging speed demons would crave more support.

Pros and Cons + All-mountain boot that loves park laps + Great cushioning and shock absorption – BOA needs frequent retightening – Beefy build

ThirtyTwo’s frills-free Lashed Double BOA walks the tightrope between power and playfulness. It gives all-mountain freestylers enough comfort for bell-to-bell riding, response for off-piste exploration, and lateral flex to flow through the park. “Cushy and comfortable,” said a longtime snowboard instructor who spends full days on her feet.

The dual-density, heat-moldable liner and light yet robust rubber outsole with integrated foam cushioning spared testers’ joints from impact. A classic dual-BOA design cinches down the tongue, and an internal ankle harness hugs the forefoot. Testers had mixed feedback on lacing: The inner lacing and BOAs work in harmony to dial fit, but we noticed some fraying of the eyelets and needed to continually tighten throughout the day. Additionally, the Lashed doesn’t have the most low-profile silhouette. But that didn’t bother our test crew too much, as the beefier build helps provide durability, warmth, and comfort. Our biggest complaint this year? One tester had a pressure point from the liner’s revamped, structured heel.

While the Lashed can be overkill for beginners in search of Sorel-level softness, after a brief break-in period, it mellows to a medium flex that’s well suited to resort ripping and freestyle applications.

Pros and Cons + Enough backbone for hard-charging + Versatile enough for all-mountain use + Comfortable and secure fit – Sloped toe caused some cap-style binding straps to slide off

One of K2’s stiffest women’s offerings, the Trance features a mid-firm backstay that speaks to all-mountain and freeride rippers. “There’s plenty of stability for freeriding, but enough flex for cruising on a pow day, too,” said a Tahoe all-mountain tester, who gave the Trance a Goldilocks flex rating: “Not too stiff, not too flexible—a great middle ground.”

We were major fans of the heat moldable and multi-density Intuition Control foam liner, as well as three-point liner lacing harness that locks it in place. One BOA dial controls the upper half of the boot, and another tightens the lower, while an articulating cuff allows the two halves of the boot to flex independently. The result? “No blisters or heel lift—my foot fits nicely, snug but not squished,” our tester said, which is especially high praise coming from someone with chronic ankle pain.

Another Tahoe rider with a wider foot agreed: “The BOA stays tight, with no pinch points, rubbing, or foot sleepiness.” She dug the lugged rubber outsole’s superior traction. However, we had one concern: Due to the sloped shape of the toe, certain binding straps designed to fit over the toe cap would slip off, no matter how much one tester tightened them.

Pros and Cons + Unbelievably adjustable + Top-tier responsiveness + Low profile – Freeriders may want a stiffer boot – May be too constricting for wide feet or high arches

Head isn’t the first to bring a triple-BOA snowboard boot to the market, but they’ve created the best integration of a dial in the liner, resulting in a perfect Cinderella fit. One BOA helps lock the heel in place, while the other two independently adjust the upper and lower shell. After heat-molding the liner, one tester was pleased to report “no pressure points, hot spots, or blisters.”

One of the biggest selling points of the PSI, though, was the asymmetrical shell, which is reinforced with aramid mesh (a key component of Kevlar) to provide a natural, intuitive all-mountain flex. “They work without thinking about them,” said a tester. The PSI earned additional kudos for a sleek, low-profile silhouette that one tester said felt as nimble as “ballerina point shoes”— a quality that was highlighted while riding and scrambling on the recycled rubber sole during a spring photo shoot.

We recommend the PSI for all-mountain riders and aggressive park rippers who like to go big in the jump line or pipe, but feel hardcore freeriders may want a touch more stiffness. Also, the liner construction and overall shape limit vertical space, making the PSI best suited to average-width and lower-volume feet. Those with wide feet or high arches may find it too constricting.

Pros and Cons + Stiff, high-performance responsiveness + Wide toe box + Durable – Stiffer than advertised – A test boot had a pressure point

Have you ever ordered “mild salsa” only to have a rogue jalapeño light your tongue on fire? That’s how we felt in the Salsa boot. While Bataleon scores the boot’s flex a 6 out of 10, we’d give it an 8 or 8.5 since testers felt Bataleon’s rating lowballed the Salsa’s stout, sturdy build and high-performance flex from the injected spine along the Achilles and a curved, firm tongue. “Highly responsive,” said a Colorado all-mountain rider. “Excellent boots for hard-charging when you want to turn on a dime.”

Our tester gave the adjustability of the double-BOA high marks, though he occasionally had to retighten the inner lacing system and found fit best for normal to medium-wide feet. “A real highlight of this boot for me is the squared-off, wide toe box, which allows my toes some breathing room laterally,” he reported. It earned additional points for its durability, showing little wear after a heavy spring. Same goes for a foam midsole that ate up landings and a Vibram outsole that handled Aspen bootpacks like a boss.

The Bataleon Salsa is available in both men’s and women’s sizes. On the men’s side, we were hyped. On the women’s side, a pressure point from the liner’s stitching made riding difficult. This was likely a one-off issue, seeing as it was in just the left boot, not the right. But it’s a good reminder that it’s always a smart idea to try boots on at your local shop or double-check return policies if you shop online.

Pros and Cons + Ultra-stiff and powerful freeride charger + Durable and long-lasting – Long break-in period – Overkill for most riders

Much like a lithe mama cheetah hell-bent on feeding her offspring, the Insano is a slim, aggressive hunter, and its prey of choice includes cliff drops and technical freeride faces. It’s also the most durable option in this guide, though breaking it in can take a week or two of hard riding.

“Insanely stiff,” signed off a hard-charging Tahoe tester. Despite its low-profile silhouette, the Insano’s TPU-heavy construction delivers power and responsiveness. Cold-resistant thermoplastic urethane bolsters the toe cap, heel counter, and steely yet smooth-flexing tongue. There’s even a TPU shank embedded into the Michelin-made, bootpack-ready outsole, stabilizing the foot and transmitting energy to your edges.  “Most aggro boots I’ve ever ridden,” applauded another tester.

The negatives are obvious: It requires significant break-in, and it’s overkill for 99.8 percent of readers (maybe more). But the 0.2 percent will appreciate the cushy multi-density foam liner and heel-locking BOA lacing on ambitious freeride missions.

Pros and Cons + Responsive charger + Removable flex stiffeners + Top-tier outsole with crampon-compatible heel welt – No walk mode for splitboarding – Pricey

Austen Sweetin’s pro model boot, the Sweetin Focus BOA is not a split-specific boot and it doesn’t have a true walk-mode. But this boot was “born to scramble,” said a Tahoe tester who claimed the molded toe cap “kicked steps like a soldier.” “If you travel frequently or just want one boot to do it all, this is hard to beat,” another tester said.

Zippered gaiters help protect against powder when bootpacking, and the relatively slim Michelin Fiberlite rubber outsoles with a carbon shank provides stability—ideal for riding between the resort and backcountry. The Focus relies exclusively on BOA lacing—not our favorite for bigger missions and multi-day trips, as field repairs are a nightmare. However, pop the upper BOA dial to loosen it for some skintrack mobility.

The Sweetin’s stout construction pairs a dual-density liner with removable stiffening inserts for “direct response on any turn initiation.” Testers praised the liner’s Velcro wrap for eliminating heel lift and recommended the boot for all-mountain riders and freeriders, calling “couloirs and big, aggressive lines” its bread and butter.

The boot’s “overbuilt” construction and exceptional durability are both pluses for backcountry riders. However, a gap between the liner and tongue near the upper calf compromised some of its responsiveness and made it incompatible with closely cropped pant legs. Still rocking the Shaun White skinnies? Keep looking.

Pros and Cons + Stellar walk mode for a soft boot + Great downhill performance + Burly outsole, reinforced toe, and heel welt for climbing – Expensive – Walk mode is poor compared to hardboots

K2’s unisex Waive is a standout on the uphill and downhill alike, providing the balance our backcountry-bound testers appreciate. Uphill, the BOA dial “frees up range of motion in the upper calf, delivering an unparalleled walk mode for a soft boot” according to a Tahoe tester. The Waive also boasts a burly, Vibram sole with a reinforced toe for bootpacking and a heel welt for semi-auto crampon compatibility—both must-have features for ridge scrambling and spring objectives.

Though hefty compared to some resort boots, the Waive is still fairly low-profile for the split-specific category. And on the descent, the Waive’s mid-stiff flex doesn’t feel too stiff or aggressive, especially once you loosen the strap and pop the BOA, testers said. “You can surf pow, no problem. But there’s plenty of performance when you batten down the hatches on top of a sketchy line,” reported that Tahoe tester, calling the Waive his ideal split boot for daily use and travel.

No real demerits here, although it’s worth noting that hardboots are much more efficient at skinning and sidehilling than soft boots. Also, the price is tough to swallow. But remember: splitboarding is cheaper than therapy!

Pros and Cons: + Great adjustability + Cushy feel – Ridiculously priced – Step On design not for most

The Waverange X Pro is a playful, comfortable, mid-soft-flexing, surf-inspired boot designed to be used exclusively with Step On bindings. (If you’re unfamiliar with the Step On system, all Step On boots feature two cleats on either side of the toe box and one connection point at the heel. These three locking points snap into place when you step onto a compatible binding.)

High-end snowboard boots trend stiffer and more responsive, speaking to more advanced all-mountain rippers and freeriders, but the Waverange X Pro is softer and more approachable, yet still packed with high-end features like triple BOA dials for adjusting fit of the upper boot, lower boot, and asymmetrical liner. “Having three BOAs really allowed fine-tuning the fit, and choosing where I want the boots to be more or less snug,” commented a Mammoth snowboard coach. Testers appreciated the grippiness of the winter-ready Vibram outsole, as well as the cushy shock absorption supplied by integrated polyurethane and gel inserts. “Felt like walking on a cloud,” said a tester.

On the descent, testers recommended the Waverange X Pro for “mellow cruiser laps,” and “playful riders” because the flex is too forgiving for aggressive riding. In pursuit of more response, multiple expert-level testers found themselves cranking the BOA aggressively, resulting in some ankle discomfort. Most testers found themselves missing their traditional strap setups, but grom-wrangling instructors and parents, beginners, and folks unable to bend down may appreciate the convenience of this Step On boot.

No piece of gear is more subjective to the rider than a pair of boots. Nothing will inform your decision-making like a visit to your local snowboard shop, as trying boots on in person is invaluable. Not to mention, boot-fitting, heat-molding, and aftermarket or custom insoles go a long way to ensure a comfortable, high-performance fit. Here are seven tried-and-true tips to make the process of shopping for snowboard boots as smooth as possible.

Shop for Boots First: If possible, shop for snowboard boots before boards and bindings. Your boot size influences both your binding size and acceptable board widths. Some boots have compact footprints, which means you’re less likely to have toe or heel drag on a narrower board. If you end up buying a boot with a bigger footprint, or you have a size 10.5 boot or higher, you may want to consider a mid-wide, wide, or volume-shifted board.

Stick to Brands You Know and Love: Every brand has a slightly different fit. Some are known for being wider or skinnier, or running bigger or smaller. If your last pair of boots fit well, consider repeating your experience with that specific brand, as chances are the fit hasn’t changed much over time. Many testers swear by the strategy of purchasing a newer version of the same boot model.

Go Wide: Many popular boot models are available in both standard sizes and wide sizes. If you have trouble squeezing into snowboard boots, or you already shop for wide sneakers or running shoes, you might want to consider a wide option.

Invest in Insoles: Even high-end snowboard boots often sport garbage insoles (as reported by a tester who fits boots for a local shop). One of the best ways to improve fit, comfort, and performance is with an aftermarket insole. We’re partial to Superfeet in most instances, but Remind Insoles aren’t a bad play if you’re looking for more shock absorption. If you really want to go the extra mile, get a custom pair from a bootfitter.

Put Your Faith in Bootfitters: There’s a misconception that only skiers need to get their boots fitted. Once you’ve had your snowboard boots professionally fit, however, you’ll never go back—especially if you have a history of foot pain. Ideally, schedule an appointment with a bootfitter who is also a snowboarder, as they’ll have a better idea of what problems you’ll face on the hill. Bootfitters can help you with everything from run-of-the-mill heat-molding to boot punches, heel-hold adjustments, liner replacements, and custom insoles.

Look for Demos, Snowboard Shops, and Return Policies: Every foot is different, so it’s worth attending demos at your local hill, where you can try boots from local shops, or visiting your local shop to try on boots in person. When you do make a purchase, support your local snowboard shop if you can. (There is a special place in hell for people who try on boots in a shop and then go home and buy them online.) If you prefer to shop online, buy from a reputable online retailer like Evo, REI, or Backcountry that has a flexible return policy.

When to Consider Step Ons: Our snowboard testers strongly prefer traditional snowboard boots to Step Ons. But if you’re battling injuries that make bending over tricky, or you are a parent or instructor wrangling groms, it can be worth considering this alternative boot-and-binding system.

This year, we sent snowboard boots to testers at their home mountains in the Wasatch, Rockies, and Sierra to put them on the chopping block all spring long. Long-term testing is crucial for picking the best snowboard boots, as break-in periods vary. A boot might be stellar out of the box, only to blow out in ten days. Or a boot might be stiff, uncomfortable, and difficult to break in for the first week, then turn into our favorite boot once it’s been out on the hill for a spell.

We encouraged testers to swap out insoles and get boots heat-molded and professionally fit—whatever they would normally do if purchasing a new pair of boots.

Once chairlifts stopped cranking and splitboarders hung up their skins for the season, we asked our test crew to fill out review forms, answering questions like: Would you purchase these boots? What rider would like these boots? Are the boots bulky or low-profile? What are your impressions on the inner and outer lacing systems?

Finally, I—test director Drew Zieff—sifted through the review forms, compared this year’s favorites to our previous, unchanged favorites from years past, and compiled these reviews on the best snowboard boots of 2027.

Drew Zieff is a Tahoe-based freelance writer and a lifelong snowboarder. Burdened with unnaturally long second toes and skinny calves and ankles, Zieff is no stranger to the boot-fitting chair (he’s a regular at Tahoe SportsHub), and he generally doesn’t trust stock insoles any more than he’ll sniff rental ones. In addition to directing Outside’s snowboard test, a role he’s handled since 2016, he directs Backcountry Magazine’s splitboard coverage and nerds out on snowboard gear and travel for Whitelines Snowboarding, REI, Gear Junkie, among others. He spends his winters testing gear in his backyard backcountry zones or up at Palisades when he’s not chasing stories and storms around the globe.

In a word, Kordell Black is a character. An esoteric ripper and veteran gear tester based in the Wasatch, Black has traveled the world with his splitboard in pursuit of powder and off-the-beaten-track adventures. He approaches big mountain lines with creative, freestyle energy, specializes in finding powder stashes overlooked by the Utah crowds, and thrashes boots into oblivion in a matter of weeks. He will also obliterate you in a flat ground game of SKATE.

Truckee’s own Jenna Shlachter is as brilliant on the hill as she is off it—which is saying something since she’s a Doctor of Psychology, after all. When she’s not on the clock, she’s usually on her snowboard, ripping everything from park to powder. Her trophy shelf needs regular reinforcement, as every year she seems to add banked slalom awards to her already impressive collection. Lucky for us, Shlachter is also an unabashed snowboard nerd, and she’s been a key contributor to our snowboard test for the last few seasons.

#8119. This Climber Just Broke Dean Potter’s Half Dome Speed Record By Free Soloing ‘Snake Dike’

Michael Reese on the summit of Half Dome after breaking the trailhead-to-summit speed record (Photo: Courtesy of Michael Reese)

On October 28, 32-year-old American climber Michael Reese set a new fastest known time on Yosemite’s Half Dome, breaking an 11-year record set by the late Dean Potter. Reese climbed the 2,000-foot batholith from the Mist Trailhead to its summit in 1 hour 12 minutes 58 seconds, following Potter’s original line up Grizzly Gully and free soloing Snake Dike (5.7 R; 800ft). He broke Potter’s previous record from May 3, 2015, by about six minutes.

Potter, who famously competed with Hans Florine to set the speed record on the Nose (5.9 C2; 3,000ft), saw the Grizzly Gully to Snake Dike line as a step toward blending trail running and climbing; he was aiming for a sub-two-hour time from trailhead to trailhead. He died 13 days after setting the record in a wingsuit accident at Taft Point.

Reese grew up in Boulder and came to climbing from running and triathlon. In September, he set a new speed record on the First Flatiron, at 7 minutes 51 seconds. After interviewing him last week in Boulder for a deep dive on the culture of free solo speed climbing, Reese told me he was headed for Yosemite the following day. I wished him luck. Having climbed both the First Flatiron and Snake Dike, I knew the latter would be a different game. The grippy, coarse sandstone of the Flatirons is a far cry from the slick, polished granite of Yosemite.

A few days after his Half Dome lap, I caught up with Reese to talk about his extensive training, the day itself, his safety margins on route, why he’s hoarded the same shoes as Potter since 2021, and why he thinks Potter’s record has stood for over a decade.

The following has been lightly edited for concision and clarity.

Michael Reese: Since I got into climbing in 2014, Dean Potter has been one of my idols, probably the one who I looked up to the most. The reason for that is he’s a hybrid athlete, you know? I come from a background in triathlon. I really like to mix cardio and strength. So Dean Potter was such an amazing individual because he had a professional-level aerobic and running fitness in addition to being one of the best free soloists, one of the best speed climbers, and one of the best BASE jumpers and highliners in the world. So I said, “Wow, how amazing is this individual to mix disciplines into territory no one’s ever seen?”

In 2021, one of Dean Potter’s good friends told me about this as a potential record to try. He became one of my main climbing partners. Of course, you know, this is 2021. Dean Potter had passed away years before. I went in 2021. I got totally destroyed because the approach was way too technical. I got lost, turned around in Grizzly Gully. It’s just such technical terrain. I went back on occasion, and started to learn the very complex approach of Grizzly Gully of alternating slabs, mazes, trees.

Bit by bit, I learned every year. I first went for a speed attempt in 2023. I went again in 2024, but I was really far off. I did 1 hour 37 [minutes] both times because it was really hard to figure out where to go. I wasn’t in as good of shape as I am in now, so I needed more fitness; I needed more practice.

Finally I came back this year, being in a lot better shape, spent two weeks practicing the route, then gave it a go.

Reese: Sixteen times before going for the record. Eight times free solo. Eight times with ropes and practicing the moves.  I practiced the crux 10 times in a row each lap, going back and forth across memorizing holds.  I didn’t really tick anything.  I jumped up and down until I purposefully would slip [while being clipped in]. I’d purposefully slip and find, “Okay, it took this amount of mistakes to actually cause a fall.”

Reese: Yes. The [complexity] of the Grizzly Gully approach, which is probably a low fifth-class approach with a lot of slabs. It has everything. It has running, it has steep, fourth-class dirt. That’s why I consider it the premier of technical mountain running, mixed running, and climbing, because you’re constantly switching gears.

Reese: We always did it a combination of simul-climbing and pitching it out. We would basically simul-climb to the crux section or sections. And then on those crux sections, I would be leading, and I would stop and [built a] traditional anchor and belay them up. That way they could give me a good belay for practicing the crux section.

Reese:  There was a lot of things that almost made it where I wouldn’t have been able to get the record. For example, I had gotten very sick just from being out in the cold. I had a cough. I had rolled my ankle two days before. So I was trying to nurse all these things, and I was just right on the fence of being like, “Am I healthy enough to go through this?”

Reese:  I’d scouted it out two days previously. Then I had a nice rest day where I just went for a picnic. I tried to ice my feet and I taped up my ankle.

My girlfriend started hiking a few hours before me to get in position because I wanted her to get some footage at the base. I hung out in Curry Village and rested. I did my typical routine where I drink a tablespoon of matcha powder to wake myself up and get amped up. I drank a ton of electrolytes because I knew that dehydration could be an issue. It was a very sunny day.

I went to the parking lot, I got on my shoes, and I put on gaiters to try to prevent a rock from going in[to my shoes in] the very dirty terrain. I had on just my watch, shoes, and shorts. No shirt because it was getting warmer. So then I did my typical warm up. I jogged for 15 minutes. I went up Grizzly Gully for a little bit to warm up my steep hiking muscles. I did some 30-second strides to get my heart rate elevated.

I  sipped some water, but tried not to overdo it, did some more strides, and then I meditated for a few minutes just to get in a good head space and say, “This is what I’ve been training for. This is my opportunity and it’s time to live in the moment.”

Reese: Not particularly. People looked at me like I was kind of crazy. Why am I sprinting back and forth at the trailhead? Why do I have no shirt when it’s 40 degrees out?

Reese:  Yeah. I connected my watch to GPS and began the effort from the Mist Trailhead on the pavement there. I had to swerve around some tourists for a minute and then I turned into Grizzly Gully. I didn’t see anyone [else] until I got to the base.

Reese:  Around noon. It was a pretty chill there, about 40 degrees. I wouldn’t mind it to warm up a little. And also because I needed to be very careful about other parties on route. Most places I could pass a party, but in a few places, like those first few pitches in the crux section, it could have been devastating to have a party on the way there.

Reese: I figured starting later would improve my chances of other parties at least being out of the crux section and a little bit further up, and, and that did luckily work out like that.

Reese:  Yeah, that’s a good question. A little bit of both. There’s a lot of places where the beta would vary so much I can’t rehearse everything. On the other hand, as you know, there’s a couple sections that the dike splits into two sections, and I do have each section rehearsed. So for the most part, I have options, and it would be okay besides that crux section. That would be pretty catastrophic.

Reese:  That’s a really good question. I do always prioritize safety. So if I came across a party and they were both in the anchor, or for example, if there was maybe just a just a follower that was securely on a tight top rope and it wouldn’t add any risk to them … and I was on record pace, I would be pretty keen to find a way to make it work, and maybe ask them just not to move, and I could tiptoe around. If there was a case where there was like a leader on the crux who was not looking solid, and I thought that going through would add risk to them or me … I would maybe bail on the attempt. Safety does come first. So yes, I would bail.

Reese:   I was going really hard, but I was saving just enough gas that I knew I wouldn’t, like, completely buckle on the crux. Then I hit the climb and felt really well. I instantly knew it was gonna be a good day on the rock. I was just kind of detecting every minuscule dish, kind of nailing the beta. And there were the people filming me at the crux section, cheering. I’d rehearsed it so much, it felt like a treat just to get across the crux and nail everything and feel really solid there. I still didn’t know if I would get it because I was gonna have to climb it faster than I ever had for the record still.

But it just flowed so well. So I did Snake Dike in 10 [minutes] 55 [seconds]. There was a special moment where I knew I would get the record because I knew I needed to finish them in, you know, 16 minutes or something. I knew I had done them in about 12 or 13 before. [That day] I did them in about 11 minutes. That Death March—that was the crux. As you know, that steep stuff after the Snake Dike, I was starting to kind of buckle, and I had a headache from dehydration. My knees and arms were starting to kind of buckle from lactic acid. But I knew I’d get the record, but I also just wanted to do the best I could and make a time that would last. So I pushed to the summit, sprinted across to the true summit, past the cables to the highest end on the north end. There was a party hanging out there.

I ran and tagged the summit, breathing hard. They were like, “Geez, dude,” like, “What did, what did you do?” I couldn’t even… My response was just dry heaving ’cause I’d gone so hard.

Reese:   The Five Ten Tennies. I bought a big stockpile of them before they went out in 2021 because I knew they were some of the best shoes and may not be made again. It’s the same ones that Dean Potter used on his attempt.

Reese:    I think the length of time honestly was kind of borderline. I think anything longer, it would be important to have something. Anything shorter, you don’t really need it. You do have a good point there. This actually was kind of a borderline scenario . Everyone’s different. For me, this one was right on the fence of bringing anything or not. And it depends on the day. If it’s a hot summer day, maybe I would change and bring something. Under the same conditions, I’m happy with not having anything.

Reese:    I think it’s because of how unique and special the line is. The magic is that most peaks, the fastest way is gonna be running around to the summit. On El Cap, the impressive nose record, you know, an hour 50… you can run around El Cap faster than that. You could run around the side and get up there in under two hours.

On Half Dome, it’s interesting, because from the Mist Trailhead to the summit, you summit up the cable. Most people go up the cables in the Subdome. So that requires running around everything, whereas Snake Dike allows a very direct line to the top.

One reason I think it’s lasted so long is Dean Potter was such an amazing athlete with his combined running and climbing. He had this high level of running combined with being able to solo Snake Dike, obviously a very easy free solo for him. So there are people that may be able to run a little bit faster, but they can’t solo Snake Dike. There are people that can solo Snake Dike, but they have nowhere near the fitness.

There have been some amazing athletes like Nick Elson from Canada.  He was able to tie Dean’s time by taking the shortcut through the forest and running around, splitting Liberty Cap and Broad Nick, shortcut through the forest to cut the switchbacks, and then up the cables.  Now everyone, including myself, starts at the Mist Trailhead. Which is an extra 60 seconds. [Editor’s note: Elson’s trailhead-to-summit time was 1 hour 20 minutes 57 seconds. He currently holds the round-trip speed record on Half Dome, with 2 hours 3 minutes 52 seconds].

When people said, “Oh, is Dean Potter’s vision really the best to go up Grizzly Gully and Snake Dike?” I think what I did proves that Dean Potter had the vision because Nick Elson, being one of the best trail runners… He’s extremely fit, one of the best athletes. I wouldn’t be able to beat his time by eight minutes to the summit off of pure fitness. So the eight-minute difference shows that Dean Potter’s line, the Grizzly Gully-Snake Dike, is just faster than the shortcut through the forest and going up cables.

Reese:    The honest answer is I don’t know. Maybe someone will get really motivated and beat it sooner rather than later. Maybe it’ll be another really long stretch. I tried to put enough of a difference where it’s gonna be a little bit hard.

Records are made to be broken. I’m not gonna be surprised if it’s broken one day. I don’t know when that’ll be. The thing is, it’ll probably have to be beaten by Grizzly Gully-Snake Dike, because it’s already been shown that some of the best trail runners can’t go under 1 hour 20 minutes by any other means running around. I think and hope it’ll have to be done by someone comfortable soloing snakes, like a runner-climber hybrid. Which makes Half Dome so special. The fastest way to the top is by climbing. It’s gotta be done by a climber.

#8118. ‘Please Help Me.’ A Hiker’s Desperate Text Led to Her Dramatic Rescue on a Famed Colorado Trail

A Black Hawk helicopter. (Photo: patty_c / Getty Images)

A desperate text to 911 turned into a dramatic rescue in the Colorado high country after an early-season storm trapped a 37-year-old solo hiker in thigh-to-hip-deep snow on the Four Pass Loop on October 30.

The Four Pass Loop is a popular but rugged 27-mile route that travels through the Maroon Bells-Snowmass Wilderness while gaining about 8,000 feet of elevation. Most hikers tackle the route as a backpacking trip over the course of two to four days.

According to a release by Crested Butte Mountain Rescue (CBMR), the ordeal began when Pitkin County Emergency Dispatch received a text to 911 that read “please help me.” Before calling for help, the hiker had texted a family member that her phone’s battery was down to 10 percent. Shortly after that initial call for help, emergency services lost contact, leaving them with only a single coordinate to guide their search. With temperatures dipping into the teens, CBMR reached out to CareFlight of the Rockies to coordinate air support. The team also dispatched a ground team, reasoning the elevation and mountain conditions could make landing a helicopter impossible.

By 11 p.m., the helicopter team located the hiker attempting to climb over Frigid Air Pass, but they were unable to make a safe landing to extract her from the scene.

About four hours later, the first two party members of the CBMR ground team reached the pass and located the hiker struggling to make it over the pass near where the helicopter had spotted her. But neither air support nor ground support could reach the hiker: “The steep terrain, deep snow, and darkness presented legitimate avalanche concerns,” CBMR wrote. “The first two rescuers initially attempted to descend toward the subject but encountered concerning conditions. Recognizing the potential hazard, they made the decision to wait for the remaining team members before committing to the descent.”

When the remaining members of the CBMR ground team reached the pass at about 5:30 a.m., two team members descended somewhere between 300 to 400 feet to reach the hiker. Upon their arrival, they realized that her condition was potentially life-threatening since she was no longer ambulatory, she had cold-related injuries, and was showing signs of hypothermia. The rescue team placed the hiker in a bivy before realizing that the best way to extract her would be via a helicopter hoist rescue.

CBMR coordinated with the Colorado Search and Rescue Association (CSAR), who contacted the Colorado Army National Guard to dispatch a UH-60 Black Hawk helicopter from Gypsum. A helicopter lowered a rescue technician to the hiker, then hoisted both party members into the helicopter.

After the hiker was successfully transferred to the airport and flown to the UCHealth Burn and Frostbite Center in Aurora, the National Guard returned to the Frigid Air Pass to remove the remaining rescuers due to the pass’s dangerous conditions.

In the wake of the incident, CBMR reminded hikers to take extra precautions before heading into the backcountry since high-altitude rescues can be dangerous for rescuers, too. (“So throw that extra puffy in your pack!” the team wrote.)

The team noted that rescue came at the end of a particularly challenging week for CBMR, which responded to three incidents, two of them fatal.

#8117. The Best Trail Running Shoes for Fall 2026

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

The best trail running shoes boost our confidence on singletrack to scree fields, sand to slick rock. They’re comfortable and nimble and help us run fast or forever, depending on the adventure. As the days grow shorter and colder we’re also looking for shoes that excel under a wide variety of circumstances, like wet leaves, rime ice, and snow. And as the weather deteriorates, we’re also leaning more on road-to-trail models for the days when the roads and paths are calling our names.

Over two to four months of testing on varied terrain across Santa Barbara to Boulder and Nebraska to New Hampshire, our testers Lisa Jhung, Cory Smith, Johnathan Beverly, and Abby Levene provided detailed feedback on fit, comfort, speed, traction, cushioning, and their joy of running. The result is Trail Runner Magazine’s best trail shoes for fall 2026. Considering that the “best” shoe can run differently on someone else’s feet, our review is specially curated with a shoe claiming the title of each chosen category it achieves best. For even more models, check out Outside’s guide to best trail running shoes for fall.

Weight: 7.5 ounces (men’s 8.5), 6.2 ounces (women’s 8) Stack Height: 28.5–21.5 mm Drop: 7 mm Sizing: 7-12.5, 13, 14, 15 (men’s), 6-11 (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Responsive and springy + Weightless feeling underfoot + Good ground feel + Excellent traction – Runs small (go half a size up) –Expensive

If the Norda 005 was a car, it would be the Mercedes AMG E63S Wagon. That is to say: it’s quiet performance luxury. IYKYK, as the kids say. Coming in at just 214 grams (7.5 ounces) for a men’s U.S. 8.5, it’s one of the lightest trail running shoes on the market. It’s also made from the highest quality materials: A Biodyneema upper makes it both durable and highly breathable. A slick of Vibram “Megagrip Elite” rubber renders the outsole ultra tacky on the trails while rolling over the roads. And, perhaps most importantly, the midsole is made completely from a proprietary Mouse Arnitel TPEE—a supercritical foam generally only used in small amounts because of the cost—making the shoe featherlight, energetic, and highly durable.

And the simplicity of the design lets the quality shine. As such, it’s a light, fast trail running shoe that can do it all. We’d turn to this shoe for anything from easy days on mixed surfaces, to “fast” trail 100-milers like Western States or Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc. Trail Runner managing editor Abby Levene wore one pair of the Norda 005 for the Tour du Mont Blanc, a five-day, 110-mile adventure through the Alps, and she didn’t think about her feet once. There is no higher praise.

The midsole is tuned to be slightly firmer than the superfoam in road racers and thus provides an energetic, bouncy ride that doesn’t trampoline you in wild directions off the trail. While the lack of a plate may disqualify the Norda 005 from being a true trail “super shoe,” don’t mistake semantics for inferiority. We didn’t miss a carbon plate here, and its absence allows for enhanced ground feel and adaptability to varied terrain. The foam and rocker deliver a smooth roll and plenty of precision.

The only real downside to this shoe is the price tag. But sometimes, you get what you pay for. Read our full review of the Norda 005.

Weight: 9.5 oz (men’s), 8.4 oz (women’s) Stack Height: 32–28 mm Drop: 4 mm Sizing: 7-13, 14, 15 (men’s), 5-12 (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Excellent traction + Lightweight and nimble – Slippery laces require double-knotting

We’ve tested every version of the Saucony Peregrine since the model’s debut in 2011, and this sixteenth iteration just might be our all-time favorite. The shoe has long been capable of making us feel nimble on rugged terrain, with its great balance of ground feel and cushioning, plus traction on all kinds of trail, wrapped up in a lightweight package. But version 16 takes the Peregrine’s trail capabilities to new levels, and at $150, it’s an easy pick for Best Value.

The upgraded Vibram Megagrip outsole grips rock slabs with aplomb, while the four-millimeter lugs dig into loose dirt and soft ground (though some sandy-trail testers craved even deeper, toothier lugs). The balanced midsole—not too springy, not too mushy, not too thick—delivers a strong connection to the trail while still feeling responsive and shock absorbing, even during wild descents. The flexible, breathable mesh upper with added toe protection kept out trail debris and warded off snags from roots and branches.

The fit of this trail running shoe somehow made a variety of testers feel like it was custom-made for them. It locks down the heel, and the just-roomy-enough toebox allowed toe space to breathe while maintaining control. “The fit is just perfect,” said a tester. “I feel secure and supported from heel to toe, and side to side.”

Weight: 10 oz (men’s), 9 oz (women’s) Stack Height: 33.5 mm–25.5 mm Drop: 8mm Sizing: 7-13, 14 (men’s), 5-11 (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Great traction + Outstanding foothold – Cushioning may feel too firm for some

The Salomon Genesis 2 earned mountain-goat status among our crew, providing outstanding traction over loose dirt and rock. Its supportive Matryx upper—constructed with thin, high-tenacity yarns and durable Kevlar—secures narrow and wide feet alike via Salomon’s quick-pull lacing system. The forefoot offers slightly more room than version 1, enhancing overall comfort without sacrificing agility.

The outsole, made of Salomon’s Contagrip rubber with toothy, 4 mm lugs, provided excellent traction on all surfaces, giving us confidence, even on scrambles over large rocky slabs and slippery descents.

While the EVA-blend midsole runs firm, it offers direct trail feedback. “This shoe makes it fun to pick a line and charge,” noted one tester. “I felt completely present instead of mindlessly rolling over obstacles.”

For technical runners who prefer softer cushioning, we also recommend the La Sportiva Prodigio Pro. (Read our full review of the La Sportiva Prodigio Pro here.)

Weight: 11.7 oz (men’s), 9.5 oz (women’s) Stack Height: 39–31 mm Drop: 8 mm Sizing: 6-15 (men’s), 5-12 (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Extremely versatile + Comfortable for all-day wear – Traction could be better

The Nike Trail Pegasus 5 has been our top choice for road-to-trail runs for several seasons, so we were concerned that its newly branded replacement, the Nike ACG Pegasus Trail, would mess with its winning formula. But as soon as we stepped into the new model, we breathed a sigh of relief. The shoe is just as comfortable as its predecessor and, after testing, has proven to be just as capable on and off roads and over gravel, continuing its reign as the most versatile shoe in this roundup.

The midsole foam—Nike’s injection-molded ReactX—feels responsive and cushions comfortably on concrete, pavement, and hard-packed dirt. The outsole traction, from 3.5 mm lugs made of the brand’s proprietary “All Terrain Compound 2.0,” is tackier on wet terrain than the previous version, but still pales in comparison to Vibram MegaGrip.

What makes this shoe work from roads to singletrack trails is the fit and foothold. Even our most narrow-footed testers felt a secure hold without any pressure points, which allows precise footing on trails, no matter how steep or rocky. This shoe’s versatility makes it a great pick as a one-trick pony for the casual runner who doesn’t need a lighter, faster race shoe, and a solid choice for travel.

Weight: 9.5 oz (unisex) Stack Height: 40–34 mm Drop: 6 mm Sizing: 5-12,13 (men’s), 6.5-13.5, 14.5 (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Extremely lightweight for a 40 mm stack + Great stability – Premium pricetag

Brooks has a reputation for building a great shoe and sticking to that formula, giving loyal fans a consistent ride, model after model. The tradeoff? It can make the brand seem boring. The all-new Brooks Cascadia Elite shatters that mold. It’s one of the most exciting shoes Brooks has launched in years, and arguably one of the most exciting trail releases of the year.

Despite sharing a name, the Cascadia Elite is nothing like the everyday, cushioned Cascadia trail runner: It’s a trail racing super shoe that is lighter, faster, and more nimble. The standout feature is the 100% PEBA midsole paired with a carbon-infused PEBAX plate that strikes a perfect balance between a springy and stable ride. On smooth, flowy single track in Santa Barbara, CA, running in the Cascadia Elite felt almost effortless, and a ton of fun.

40 millimeters under the heel is a lot of foam to deal with, but the ride never felt squishy or overly bouncy in off-camber footing. A wide platform, paired with a flexible, embedded horseshoe-shaped plate, keeps the Cascadia Elite from being tippy. That width does come at a cost, though; picking tight lines through technical terrain requires precise footing to keep from getting wedged between rocks.

If you’re in the market for a trail running shoe, first consider the type of trails you run on regularly: do you tackle rugged, mountainous terrain, or stick to mellow dirt paths? Some trail shoes can handle both adequately, while others are specialized and excel in one or the other. Shoes with smaller lugs are generally better on smoother, firmer terrain, whereas shoes with deeper, more aggressive outsoles are optimized for steep, muddy, or rocky trails. If you like to feel the trail and dance around rocks and roots, you’ll likely prefer a light, more minimal shoe, but if you’d rather let the shoe roll over trail variations, cushioning and protecting while you zone out, you should look for a shoe with a thicker midsole.

Once you’ve narrowed the search to a certain type of trail shoe, you need to find a pair that complements your unique body and stride. Every runner’s body, gait, speed, experience, and ride preferences are different, so every runner will interact differently with each trail shoe. The shoe that your best friend or your sister-in-law loves may be uncomfortable for you and make running feel slow, sluggish, or even painful. Finding the perfect pair of trail running shoes is a seriously personal affair.

The process for choosing the best running shoes is a matter of finding the models that both fit your foot and also feel best when you’re running. To determine fit and feel, there’s no substitute for trying the shoes on and running in them.

When assessing fit, first pay attention to length. You need room at the end of your toes as your feet lengthen during their dynamic movements on the run. A rule of thumb is to allow a thumb’s width between your longest toe and the end of the shoe. Runners often wear a running shoe a half or full size bigger than their street shoes.

Ensure that the shape of the sole and the upper matches your foot shape. The sole should be as wide or wider than your foot for the whole length, and match the curve of your arch comfortably. The shoe should hold your foot securely over the instep, while allowing the ball of the foot and the toes to splay and flex when you roll forward onto them. Your heel shouldn’t slip when you lift it, and the arch should be able to dome and lengthen naturally. Nothing should bind or rub as you roll through the stride.

If the shoe fits, it’s time to take them on a short run on a treadmill, around the store, or, ideally, down the block and back. Every trail running shoe has a unique ride created by the type and density of foam in the midsole and the geometry of that foam: its thickness, width, heel-to-toe drop, molded sidewalls or flares, and forefoot flexibility or rocker shape (plus, in an increasing number of models, the presence of and type of embedded plate). Each of these elements interact with each other and your stride to determine how the shoe reacts on landing, how much it cushions, how stably it supports, how smoothly it transitions from landing to toe off, and how quickly and powerfully it rebounds.

The best way to choose trail running shoes that complement your body and stride is to find the ones that feel right on the run. Benno Nigg, the world-leading biomechanics professor who proposed this method of shoe selection, calls it the “comfort filter,” but makes clear it is far more than how plush the shoe feels when you step into it. What you want to assess is whether the shoe allows and supports the way your feet want to move, what Nigg calls your “preferred movement path.” In the right shoe, while running at your normal pace, you will touch down where you expect to land, roll smoothly and stably through the stride without noticing the shoe, feel both cushioned from and connected to the ground, and push off naturally, quickly, and powerfully. When this comes together you’ll know that you’ve found your pair.

It’s likely that several shoes will feel good on your feet. To find the most comfortable, it helps to compare them back to back, like an eye doctor will do with corrective lenses: flipping between “A” or “B,” “1” or “2.” You may also find that different shoes feel better at different paces or level of fatigue, and you may want more than one pair. In fact, research shows that wearing a variety of different shoes is one of the few proven ways to reduce injury risk as it appears to vary the stresses on your feet and joints.

Running shoes have long been marketed and sold as prescriptive devices to help runners stay healthy, but there is little scientific evidence correlating shoes, or any specific shoe properties—like cushioning or pronation control—with running injuries. Medical professionals say that it is highly difficult to determine whether a runner needs a certain type of shoe, and studies have shown that prescribing shoes using traditional methods like treadmill gait analyses or wet-foot arch height tests don’t consistently reduce injuries.

Don’t assume that you need more cushioning or more stability if you have sore joints, or if you’re a heavier runner, or if you’re a beginner—evidence doesn’t support many common beliefs. The best way prevent injury is find two or three different pairs that feel right on the run, ease into using them, and vary your shoes, your running surface and your pace regularly (plus avoid rapid increases in your training load and work on improving your mechanics).

Each season, we evaluate new releases from top outdoor brands, distributing samples to testers based on foot shape and local trail conditions and preferences. For this fall update, we evaluated 5 new models alongside 91 previously tested shoes to select the best trail running shoes on the market.

Over two to four months of testing on varied terrain across the country (from Santa Barbara to Boulder, Nebraska to New Hampshire), our team provided detailed feedback on fit, comfort, traction, cushioning, and responsiveness. We combined these reports with our own trail testing to select category winners and top recommendations for every type of runner.

Freelance journalist, editor, and author Lisa Jhung has researched, tested, and written about running shoes for the past decade and a half, much of that time for Outside. She coordinates a fleet of female shoe testers out of Boulder, Colorado, and says her home office is a perpetual obstacle course of cardboard boxes and piles of running shoes. Lisa’s written about gear of all kinds for numerous national magazines as both an editor and freelancer, including a stint as the shoes and gear blogger and trail running microsite editor for Runner’s World.

A high school jumper and occasional sprinter/hurdler, she started running—really running—after walking off the collegiate volleyball team, and moved on to road and trail races of any distance, triathlons, adventure races, and mountain running. She’s happiest testing rugged trail shoes on gnarly terrain, and also loves a good neighborhood jaunt…but is almost always looking for ribbons of dirt. Lisa is the author of Running That Doesn’t Suck: How to Love Running (Even if You Think You Hate It) and Trailhead: The Dirt on All Things Trail Running.

Cory’s passion for running started over 30 years ago in high school when he became the number six ranked runner in the nation at 3000 meters his senior year. After high school, he competed at Villanova University, earning two NCAA Division I Championship showings. Today, he’s determined not to let age slow him down and competes on the national master’s circuit, running a 4:12 (4:30 mile pace) 1500 meters and 9:04 (4:52 mile pace) 3000 meters in 2021 at age 43. He prefers a hard track workout or tempo run over an easy long run any day but also appreciates a challenging trail or mountain run.

His obsession with running shoes started in 2014 when he wrote his first shoe review for Gear Institute. Since then, he’s tested and reviewed hundreds of running shoes, clothing, and gear for Outside, Runner’s World, Footwear News, and other outlets. He has a soft spot for speedy shoes over heavy trainers but loves dissecting all shoes equally and thinking like a product engineer to explain the why behind every design detail. Cory is the Founder of Run Your Personal Best, an online running coaching business, and since its inception in 2014, has coached runners to over 100 Boston Marathon Qualifying times.

Jonathan fell in love with running his freshman year of high school and quickly became fascinated with finding the perfect pair of running shoes. That quest got a boost when he became editor of Running Times in 2000 and started receiving every new model as they were released. The parade of shoes continued while he served as shoe editor for Runner’s World, then editor of PodiumRunner, and currently fitness gear editor at Outside. Having now worn nearly every running shoe created in this century—and a fair amount of those dating back to the early models of the ’70s—he’s given up on finding the one best and now relishes the wide variety of excellent options.

Once a 2:46 marathoner regularly doing 50+ mile weeks, recent injuries and his age have reduced his volume and slowed his pace—but he still enjoys an uptempo workout or two each week. Beverly is the author of the book Your Best Stride which explores how each individual’s gait—and thus shoe preference—is unique. He enjoys getting scientists’ take on new shoe trends and trying to describe the nuances of each shoe’s ride.

#8116. A Hiker Slid Hundreds of Feet Down Mount Timpanogos. Newly Released Video Shows the Harrowing Rescue.

A hiker slid hundreds of feet down Utah's Mount Timpanogos while hiking in late October (Photo: UCSO)

Newly released helicopter footage shows the dramatic moment rescuers saved a hiker who fell from the summit of Mount Timpanogos, a 11,700-foot peak in Utah’s Wasatch Range.

On October 26, a female hiker fell off the trail and slid several hundred feet from the peak. She landed on a small ledge on a cliff, according to the Utah County Sheriff’s Office (UCSO). Authorities have not released the woman’s name or age.

“We have heard that the hiker is recovering well from her injuries, and we wish her a full and speedy recovery,” the agency wrote in a statement on November 3. “Thank you to all those agencies that rushed to the rescue. This incident is a stark reminder of how fast a fun outing can turn into a life-or-death situation.”

About 50 miles from Salt Lake City, Mount Timpanogos is accessible via two strenuous trails: Timpooneke and Aspen Grove. Both trails are roughly 14 miles out-and-back and cross snowfields and steep scree fields. Day hikes often take between eight and 12 hours, according to Explore Utah Valley.

While Timpanogos is a popular late-summer day hike, snowstorms can sweep through the high-elevation summit beginning in late September, making trail conditions unpredictable and sometimes dangerous.

The video shows the mountain summit where the hiker started their trek, the steep slope they slid down, and the small ledge where they stopped. According to the UCSO, search-and-rescue crews initially spotted the woman from an airplane before sending in the Utah Department of Public Safety Helicopter Crew helicopter to hoist her to an awaiting ambulance.

“The hiker was badly injured during the fall and was taken by Lone Peak Fire Department to the Utah Valley Hospital,” the UCSO wrote in an October 26 Facebook post.

The responding agencies remind hikers to use extreme caution when recreating in high elevations where snow and ice are present. In the late fall, snow can melt and refreeze, turning trails into icy ramps. Knowing how to self-arrest with an ice axe and carrying mountaineering gear is essential.

“We are extremely grateful for the outcome of today’s rescue and our awesome partners,” UCSO said.
